Electron Spin Resonance in S=1/2S=1/2 antiferromagnetic chains

Masaki Oshikawa1 and Ian Affleck2 Note:  On leave from Department of Physics and Astronomy and Canadian Institute for Advanced Research, The University of British Columbia, Vancouver, B.C., V6T 1Z1, Canada Address: 1Department of Physics, Tokyo Institute of Technology, Oh-okayama, Meguro-ku, Tokyo 152-8551, Japan
2Department of Physics, Boston University, Boston, MA 02215
August 13, 2001
Abstract

A systematic field-theory approach to Electron Spin Resonance (ESR) in the S=1/2S=1/2 quantum antiferromagnetic chain at low temperature TT (compared to the exchange coupling JJ) is developed. In particular, effects of a transverse staggered field hh and an exchange anisotropy (including a dipolar interaction) δ\delta on the ESR lineshape are discussed. In the lowest order of perturbation theory, the linewidth is given as ∝J​h2/T2\propto Jh^{2}/T^{2} and ∝(δ/J)2​T\propto(\delta/J)^{2}T, respectively. In the case of a transverse staggered field, the perturbative expansion diverges at lower temperature; non-perturbative effects at very low temperature are discussed using exact results on the sine-Gordon field theory. We also compare our field-theory results with the predictions of Kubo-Tomita theory for the high-temperature regime, and discuss the crossover between the two regimes. It is argued that a naive application of the standard Kubo-Tomita theory to the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction gives an incorrect result. A rigorous and exact identity on the polarization dependence is derived for certain class of anisotropy, and compared with the field-theory results.

I Introduction

Quantum spin chains have been studied extensively for both their experimental and theoretical interests. Among many experimental methods of investigation, Electron Spin Resonance (ESR) is unique for its high sensitivity to anisotropy. While the theory of ESR has been studied[1, 2, 3, 4] for a long time, there remain important open problems, especially for strongly interacting systems. One of the problems is that, generally one has to make a crucial assumption about the lineshape at some point during the calculation. As we will demonstrate, such an assumption could be incorrect in some cases although it might have been taken for granted in the literature. In addition, in an actual calculation one has to calculate various correlation functions. Traditionally, crude approximations such as the high-temperature approximation, the classical spin approximation and the decoupling of the correlation functions are used. However, these approximations break down when the many-body correlation effects are strong. As a consequence, rather little has been understood about ESR when many-body correlations become important. Even in the cases which were believed to be understood with the existing theories, there appear to be subtle problems.

In this paper, we study ESR in S=1/2S=1/2 quantum spin chains in the “one-dimensional critical region” where the temperature TT is sufficiently small compared to the characteristic energy of the exchange interaction JJ (but TT is still large compared to three-dimensional ordering temperature or spin-Peierls transition temperature.) We stress that ESR in such a region is essentially a many-body problem. Here, many of the traditional theoretical techniques lose their validity. Instead, (1+1)(1+1)-dimensional field theory should describe the universal, low-energy/large-distance behavior. Our main purpose in the present paper is to develop a new approach to ESR based on field theory (bosonization) methods. At least for several simple cases (which are of experimental interest) we are able to formulate the problem in terms of the systematic Feynman-Dyson perturbation theory, avoiding previously made ad hoc assumptions. We will study several consequences of our theory for two types of perturbations of the one-dimensional S=1/2S=1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet: a staggered field, and an exchange anisotropy (or dipolar interaction). When the effect of the anisotropy is small, the ESR lineshape is shown to be Lorentzian up to a possible small smooth background; the width and the shift of the Lorentzian peak are given perturbatively. In one dimension, it was argued that the diffusive spin dynamics leads to a non-Lorentzian lineshape, which is indeed observed in the S=5/2S=5/2 antiferromagnetic chain TMMC[4]. However, our results imply that the argument does not apply to the present case of the S=1/2S=1/2 antiferromagnetic chain at low temperature.

In a compound with a low crystal symmetry permitting a staggered component of the gyromagnetic tensor or a staggered Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction, an effective staggered field is also produced by the applied uniform field. The staggered field corresponds to a relevant operator in the Renormalization Group sense, and is related to the field-induced gap phenomenon recently found in several quasi-one dimensional S=1/2S=1/2 antiferromagnets[5, 6, 8, 9]. Since it is a relevant operator, one may expect that its effect is enhanced at lower temperatures. Indeed, we find that the staggered field contributes to the linewidth proportionally to h2/T2h^{2}/T^{2} where hh is the magnitude of the staggered field. We propose this as an explanation of the peculiar low-temperature behavior[10] found in ESR on Cu Benzoate nearly 30 years ago. Moreover, we propose that the sharp resonance found at very low temperature[11], which was understood as a signature of a three-dimensional Néel ordering, may well be understood in a purely one-dimensional framework based on sine-Gordon field theory.

On the other hand, dipolar interactions or exchange anisotropies are present in virtually any real material. We find that their contribution to the linewidth is proportional to TT, which appears to be consistent with existing experimental data on several quasi one dimensional S=1/2S=1/2 antiferromagnet such as CuGeO3, KCuF3 and NaV2O5.

Basic ideas and some of the results in the present paper were presented briefly in Ref. 12. This paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we briefly review the basics of ESR in interacting spin systems, including a few (apparently) new results, namely an exact and rigorous identity on the polarization dependence, and the relation between the Kubo-Tomita[1] and the Mori-Kawasaki[2, 3] theories. In Sections III and  V we develop a new framework for studying ESR in quantum spin chains, based on field theory methods and, in particular, the Dyson formula expressing the Green’s function for a scalar field in terms of the self-energy. It is applied in Sections IV, VI, VII and  VIII to systems with an exchange anisotropy (or dipolar interaction) or a transverse staggered field. (The case of an exchange anisotropy with the axis parallel to the field turns out to be easier to treat and not to require the self-energy formalism. Therefore it is treated first, in Section IV.) In Section IX, we compare our results to those in the high-temperature regime obtained with the previous approach. Section X is devoted to conclusions. Appendix A contains an alternative derivation of an old formula for the width/shift first derived by Mori and Kawasaki [2, 3].

II Electron Spin Resonance

II.1 Definition of the problem

A single spin in a magnetic field HH has energy levels separated by the Zeeman energy EZ=g​μB​HE_{Z}=g\mu_{B}H. If an electromagnetic wave of angular frequency ω\omega is applied to such a system, resonant absorption occurs when ℏ​ω=EZ\hbar\omega=E_{Z} and the polarization (direction of the oscillating magnetic field) is perpendicular to the static field. When the spins are coupled by interactions, the physics is of course not that simple. However, generally some resonant absorption occurs also in the interacting system. This is the phenomenon of ESR which we study in the present paper. In an interacting system, it is also possible to observe absorption of the electromagnetic wave polarized parallel to the static magnetic field (so called Voigt configuration.) In this paper, we focus on the standard (Faraday) configuration, which measures the absorption of the electromagnetic wave polarized perpendicular to the static magnetic field.

Assuming that the absorption can be described by linear response theory, the absorption intensity I⁡(ω)I(\omega) per volume for the radiation linearly polarized in the α⟂z\alpha\perp z direction is given by

I⁡(ω)=HR2​ω2​χα​α′′​(q=0,ω),I(\omega)=\frac{{H_{R}}^{2}\omega}{2}\chi^{\prime\prime}_{\alpha\alpha}(q=0,\omega), (1)

where HRH_{R} is the amplitude of the radiation and χ′′\chi^{\prime\prime} is the imaginary part of the dynamical magnetic susceptibility. χ′′\chi^{\prime\prime} is related to the retarded Green’s function 𝒢R{\cal G}^{R} as

χα​β′′​(q,ω)=−Im​𝒢α​βR​(q,ω),\chi^{\prime\prime}_{\alpha\beta}(q,\omega)=-{\rm Im}{\cal G}^{R}_{\alpha\beta}(q,\omega), (2)

where 𝒢α​βR{\cal G}^{R}_{\alpha\beta} is defined by

𝒢α​βR(q,ω)=−i∫0∞dt∑x⟨[Sα(x,t),Sβ(0,0)]⟩e−i​q​x+i​ω​t{\cal G}^{R}_{\alpha\beta}(q,\omega)=-i\int_{0}^{\infty}dt\sum_{x}\langle[S^{\alpha}(x,t),S^{\beta}(0,0)]\rangle e^{-iqx+i\omega t} (3)

where ⟨…⟩\langle\ldots\rangle is the statistical average at temperature TT. In most experiments, the applied electromagnetic wave is typically in the microwave regime, and its wavelength is very large compared to all relevant length scales in the antiferromagnet since the spin-wave velocity is much less than the speed of light. Thus, in ESR, the dynamical susceptibility is measured at essentially zero momentum q=0q=0. ESR probes the dynamics of the system only at the special momentum q=0q=0, in contrast to neutron scattering which can be used to scan momentum space. However, as we will explain below, there is an interesting feature at the special momentum q=0q=0. Together with the relatively easy availability of highly precise data, ESR offers a unique insight into magnetic systems which would be difficult to obtain with other experimental methods.

A remarkable feature of ESR is that, if the Hamiltonian of the system (apart from the Zeeman term) is isotropic (ie. S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetric), the resonance is still at the Zeeman energy and completely sharp, as if there is no interaction at all. This result can be deduced rather easily from the equation of motion, as we will show in the following. Throughout this paper, we take the direction of the static applied field as the zz-axis. Let us consider the total Hamiltonian

ℋ=ℋ0+ℋZ,{\cal H}={\cal H}_{0}+{\cal H}_{Z}, (4)

where ℋZ=−H∑jSzj{\cal H}_{Z}=-H\sum_{j}S^{z}_{j} is the Zeeman term and ℋ0{\cal H}_{0} is the exchange Hamiltonian which is assumed to be S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetric. We choose units so that ℏ=g​μB=1\hbar=g\mu_{B}=1 except where explicitly mentioned otherwise; these constants can be recovered by dimensional analysis. We also assume HH is much smaller than the exchange coupling JJ (ie. energy scale of ℋ0{\cal H}_{0}). As we have mentioned above, in ESR the electromagnetic wave is coupled to the q=0q=0 component of the spin operators, namely the total spin operators Sα=∑jSjαS^{\alpha}=\sum_{j}S^{\alpha}_{j}. The Heisenberg equation of motion for S+=Sx+i​SyS^{+}=S^{x}+iS^{y} reads

d​S+d​t=i⁡[ℋ,S+]=i⁡[ℋZ,S+]=−i​H​S+,\frac{dS^{+}}{dt}=i[{\cal H},S^{+}]=i[{\cal H}_{Z},S^{+}]=-iHS^{+}, (5)

because ℋ0{\cal H}_{0} commutes with S+S^{+} due to the S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry of ℋ0{\cal H}_{0}. It follows that S+​(t)=S+​e−i​H​tS^{+}(t)=S^{+}e^{-iHt}, and consequently χ+⁣−​(0,ω)∝δ⁡(ω−H)\chi^{+-}(0,\omega)\propto\delta(\omega-H). This means that the resonance is completely sharp, and located exactly at the Zeeman energy. Namely, this resonance has the lineshape identical to ESR in a single (non-interacting) spin in spite of an arbitrary strong exchange interaction. On the other hand, the absorption intensity is generally affected by the exchange interaction ℋ0{\cal H}_{0}. For example, in a spin-gap system at zero temperature, the absorption intensity is zero if the applied field HH is smaller than the gap.

As we have seen, the completely sharp resonance is related to the S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry of the exchange Hamiltonian ℋ0{\cal H}_{0}. While it is natural that symmetries of the system are important in determining the dynamics of the system, the present situation is rather unique, for the S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry is explicitly broken down to U⁡(1)U(1) by the applied static field but is still essential in ESR. This peculiar feature is related to the fact that the applied field couples to the total magnetization Sz=∑jSjzS^{z}=\sum_{j}S^{z}_{j}, which is a generator of the global S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry and is conserved under ℋ0{\cal H}_{0}. Since the total magnetization and Hamiltonian are simultaneously diagonalizable, the applied field does not change the eigenstates of the system, if they are classified by SzS^{z}. The only effect of the static applied field is to shift the energy levels of the eigenstates; the shifted energy levels still reflects the S​U​(2)SU(2) multiplet structure. This kind of “weak” symmetry breaking by one of the symmetry generators preserves some structures of the fully symmetric system. In ESR of an isotropic system ℋ0{\cal H}_{0}, the S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry is only weakly broken and is essential in determining the ESR spectrum.

A similar application of the concept of weakly broken global symmetry was also exploited recently by S. C. Zhang[13] in his S​O​(5)SO(5) theory of high-TcT_{c} superconductivity. Namely, in the S​O​(5)SO(5) theory, the most important terms in the effective Hamiltonian are S​O​(5)SO(5) symmetric one and the chemical potential couples to one of the generators of the global S​O​(5)SO(5) symmetry. The so-called π\pi-excitation in this context is a sharp resonance which is similar to ESR in isotropic spin systems.

In real magnetic systems, there are various types of anisotropy, such as the dipolar interaction. Let us write the total Hamiltonian as

ℋ=ℋ0+ℋ′+ℋZ,{\cal H}={\cal H}_{0}+{\cal H}^{\prime}+{\cal H}_{Z}, (6)

where ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime} is the symmetry-breaking perturbation. Throughout this paper, we assume the interaction to be nearly isotropic, namely that ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime} is small compared to the other terms ℋ0{\cal H}_{0} and ℋZ{\cal H}_{Z}. Once the perturbation ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime} is added, the argument leading to the delta-function resonance at the Zeeman energy breaks down. Thus, in general, the addition of ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime} causes changes in the lineshape, such as a broadening and a shift of the resonance. The main theoretical problem is then to calculate the absorption spectrum for the given Hamiltonian ℋ{\cal H} and other conditions such as the temperature of the system.

II.2 Previous theories

The existing approaches to ESR, such as those of Kubo and Tomita [1] and of Mori and Kawasaki [2, 3] were developed mainly during 1950s-60s. Here we summarize briefly, a part of those achievements which is closely related to our analysis.

When the isotropic exchange interactions between spins are weak, namely ℋ0{\cal H}_{0} is much smaller than ℋZ{\cal H}_{Z}, the lineshape is generally expected to be Gaussian. On the other hand, once the anisotropy ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime} is present, strong isotropic exchange interactions ℋ0{\cal H}_{0} between spins affects the ESR lineshape, even though it does not break the S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry by itself. In the presence of the strong interaction (ℋ0≫ℋZ{\cal H}_{0}\gg{\cal H}_{Z}), which applies to the problem considered in this paper, the lineshape is generally expected to be Lorentzian. (On the other hand, the lineshape is believed to be neither Gaussian nor Lorentzian, when the spin diffusion is dominant. [4]) The effect of the isotropic exchange interactions on the lineshape has been traditionally called Exchange Narrowing. We emphasize that ESR in such an interacting spin system probes the collective motion of the many-body system. In this paper, we focus on this limit of strong isotropic exchange interaction, while other cases have been discussed previously as well [1, 2, 3].

For the case of the Lorentzian lineshape, Mori and Kawasaki[2] proposed a formula, which we call the MK formula, for the linewidth η\eta:

η=12​χu​H​Im​[−G𝒜𝒜†R​(ω=H)],\eta=\frac{1}{2\chi_{u}H}{\rm Im}{[-G^{R}_{{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}}(\omega=H)]}, (7)

where χu\chi_{u} is the magnetic susceptibility and G𝒜𝒜†R​(ω)G^{R}_{{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}}(\omega) is the Fourier transform of the unperturbed retarded Green’s function

G𝒜𝒜†R​(t)=−i​θ​(t)​⟨[𝒜⁡(t),𝒜†​(0)]⟩0,G^{R}_{{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}}(t)=-i\theta(t)\langle[{\cal A}(t),{\cal A}^{\dagger}(0)]\rangle_{0}, (8)

where ⟨…⟩0\langle\ldots\rangle_{0} is the expectation value under the unperturbed Hamiltonian ℋ0+ℋZ{\cal H}_{0}+{\cal H}_{Z}, θ⁡(t)\theta(t) is the step function, and 𝒜{\cal A} is defined by the commutator

𝒜=[ℋ′,S+].{\cal A}=[{\cal H}^{\prime},S^{+}]. (9)

In this paper, 𝒢{\cal G} refers to a full Green’s function calculated using the Hamiltonian including the perturbation ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime}, while GG denotes the unperturbed Green’s function evaluated in the absence of the perturbation. Both kinds of Green’s functions (𝒢{\cal G} and GG) should be evaluated including the Zeeman term ℋZ{\cal H}_{Z}, in the original spin chain context. However, as we will see in Section III, in the effective field theory, the Zeeman term is absorbed by a momentum shift. Thus, the Green’s functions in the effective field theory will be defined without explicitly including the Zeeman term.

In addition to the broadening, the perturbation ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime} also causes a shift of the resonance energy; the shift is given by

Δ​ω=−12​χu​H​{⟨[𝒜,S−]⟩−Re​G𝒜𝒜†R​(ω=H)}.\Delta\omega=\frac{-1}{2\chi_{u}H}\left\{\langle[{\cal A},S^{-}]\rangle-{\rm Re}G^{R}_{{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}}(\omega=H)\right\}. (10)

This formula for the shift is slightly different from the one given in the original paper[2]. We believe that ours is the correct one in the lowest order of perturbation theory.

The derivation of the MK formulae in the original paper seems somewhat involved, and it is not clear to us what assumptions are necessary to prove them. However, we found that the MK formulae is indeed exact in the lowest order of the perturbation theory, if the (single) Lorentzian lineshape is assumed. Explicitly speaking, we must assume:

𝒢S+​S−R​(ω)=2​⟨Sz⟩ω−H−Σ,{\cal G}^{R}_{S^{+}S^{-}}(\omega)=\frac{2\langle S^{z}\rangle}{\omega-H-\Sigma}, (11)

where Σ\Sigma is a smooth function of ω\omega near ω=H\omega=H. Regarding Σ\Sigma as a constant near the resonance, we obtain a Lorentzian line-shape. [Setting Σ=0\Sigma=0 in Eq. (11) gives the exact result for the isotropic case ℋ′=0{\cal H}^{\prime}=0.] The simple, and possibly new, alternative derivation using the equation of motion is presented in Appendix A.

On the other hand, Kubo and Tomita[1] studied ESR using a somewhat different formulation. For the case of Lorentzian lineshape, their theory gives the following formula for the linewidth, at high temperature:

η∼1|J|​⟨𝒜𝒜†⟩⟨S+​S−⟩,\eta\sim\frac{1}{|J|}\frac{\langle{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}\rangle}{\langle S^{+}S^{-}\rangle}, (12)

where the expectation value is the static correlation function. We shall call this the KT formula in this paper. We could not find in the literature how the two formulae (7) and (12) are related. On the other hand, if the KT formula (12) for the Lorentzian lineshape is indeed valid at high temperature, it must be consistent with the MK formula. In fact, we have verified that the KT formula (12) follows from the high-temperature limit of the MK formula (7) with a certain assumption. The derivation is given as follows. Taking the Fourier transform of eq. (8), at temperature TT,

G𝒜𝒜†R(ω)=−iZ∫0∞dtei​ω​tTr([𝒜(t),𝒜†(0)]e−(ℋ0+ℋZ)/T),G^{R}_{{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}}(\omega)=-\frac{i}{Z}\int_{0}^{\infty}dte^{i\omega t}{\rm Tr}{\left([{\cal A}(t),{\cal A}^{\dagger}(0)]e^{-({\cal H}_{0}+{\cal H}_{Z})/T}\right)}, (13)

where Z=Tre−(ℋ0+ℋZ)/TZ={\rm Tr}{e^{-({\cal H}_{0}+{\cal H}_{Z})/T}}. Expanding this up to the first order in 1/T1/T, we find,

G𝒜𝒜†R​(ω)\displaystyle G^{R}_{\cal A{\cal A}^{\dagger}}(\omega) ∼\displaystyle\sim iT​Z∞​∫0∞d​t​Tr​([ℋ0+ℋZ,𝒜⁡(t)]​𝒜†​(0))​ei​ω​t\displaystyle\frac{i}{TZ_{\infty}}\int_{0}^{\infty}dt{\rm Tr}{\left([{\cal H}_{0}+{\cal H}_{Z},{\cal A}(t)]{\cal A}^{\dagger}(0)\right)}e^{i\omega t} (14)
=\displaystyle= 1T​Z∞​∫0∞d​t​Tr​(d​𝒜d​t​(t)​𝒜†​(0))​ei​ω​t\displaystyle\frac{1}{TZ_{\infty}}\int_{0}^{\infty}dt{\rm Tr}{\left(\frac{d{\cal A}}{dt}(t){\cal A}^{\dagger}(0)\right)}e^{i\omega t}
=\displaystyle= −1T​Z∞​Tr​[𝒜⁡(0)​𝒜†​(0)]−i​ωT​Z∞​∫0∞d​t​Tr​[𝒜⁡(t)​𝒜†​(0)]​ei​ω​t,\displaystyle-\frac{1}{TZ_{\infty}}{\rm Tr}\left[{{\cal A}(0){\cal A}^{\dagger}(0)}\right]-i\frac{\omega}{TZ_{\infty}}\int_{0}^{\infty}dt{\rm Tr}\left[{{\cal A}(t){\cal A}^{\dagger}(0)}\right]e^{i\omega t},

where the time evolution is defined with respect to the unperturbed Hamiltonian ℋ0+ℋZ{\cal H}_{0}+{\cal H}_{Z} and Z∞=Tr​1Z_{\infty}={\rm Tr}1 is the partition function in the infinite temperature limit. The first term is real and does not contribute to the imaginary part. If we assume that the dynamical correlation function at infinite temperature Tr⁡[𝒜†​(t)​𝒜​(0)]{\rm Tr}\left[{{\cal A}^{\dagger}(t){\cal A}(0)}\right] decays exponentially with the characteristic time τc∼1/J\tau_{c}\sim 1/J, the second term gives −i​ωJ​T​⟨𝒜†​(0)​𝒜​(0)⟩∞-i\frac{\omega}{JT}\langle{{\cal A}^{\dagger}(0){\cal A}(0)}\rangle_{\infty}, where ⟨⟩∞\langle\rangle_{\infty} is the expectation value at the infinite temperature and we use ω≪J\omega\ll J. We note that a similar assumption was made also in the original derivation of eq. (12) in the Kubo-Tomita paper. Thus the MK formula (7) reduces, in the high-temperature limit, to

η∼⟨𝒜𝒜†⟩∞2​χu​T​J.\eta\sim\frac{\langle{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}\rangle_{\infty}}{2\chi_{u}TJ}. (15)

Because ⟨S+​S−⟩∼2​χu​T\langle S^{+}S^{-}\rangle\sim 2\chi_{u}T in the high-temperature limit, this is equivalent to the KT formula (12). We note that, because τc∼1/J\tau_{c}\sim 1/J is valid only as an order-of-magnitude estimate at best, the KT formula has the uncertainty of an overall constant factor.

Recently, a numerical approach to ESR in quantum spin chains is also being developed[14] by a direct calculation of the dynamical susceptibility χ′′​(ω)\chi^{\prime\prime}(\omega). Since it is based on an exact diagonalization of the full spectrum of short chains, it is restricted to rather short chain of up to 10 spins even for S=1/2S=1/2, making finite size effects rather severe. On the other hand, the direct numerical calculation is applicable at any temperature. In contrast, the field theory approach, which we will develop in the present paper, is valid only at low temperatures while it is based on the thermodynamic limit. Thus they are complementary to each other.

We remark that some results quite closely related to ours were derived by Giamarchi and Millis[30, 31] in their work on the ac conductivity of a Tomonaga-Luttinger (TL) liquid. We will comment on the connections with our work later.

II.3 Polarization dependence

When observing ESR in the Faraday configuration, the polarization of the electromagnetic wave is perpendicular to the direction of the static magnetic field, which we take as the zz-axis. There are still two independent possible polarizations; the linear polarization can take any direction in the x​yxy-plane. Except when the total Hamiltonian ℋ{\cal H} is invariant under a rotation about the zz axis, the absorption spectrum generally depends on the polarization. Within the linear response theory, the dependence comes from the difference between the dynamical susceptibility χx​x′′​(0,ω)≠χy​y′′​(0,ω)\chi^{\prime\prime}_{xx}(0,\omega)\neq\chi^{\prime\prime}_{yy}(0,\omega). The MK formula ignores the possible polarization dependence, because it deals with χ+⁣−′′∼χx​x′′+χy​y′′\chi^{\prime\prime}_{+-}\sim\chi^{\prime\prime}_{xx}+\chi^{\prime\prime}_{yy}, and not χx​x′′\chi^{\prime\prime}_{xx} and χy​y′′\chi^{\prime\prime}_{yy} separately. The polarization dependence was discussed theoretically first by Natsume et al. [15, 16, 17] generalizing the Kubo-Tomita theory. It has also been observed experimentally [15, 16] and numerically [14].

However, apparently it has been not recognized that, for some special cases, an exact and rigorous result on the polarization dependence can be derived easily from the equation of motion. Let us consider the special case in which the perturbation ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime} is written in terms of the xx component of the spin operator SjxS^{x}_{j}. The examples include the transverse staggered field ℋ′=h​∑j(−1)j​Sjx{\cal H}^{\prime}=h\sum_{j}(-1)^{j}S^{x}_{j}, and the exchange anisotropy with the anisotropy axis in the xx direction ℋ′=δ​∑jSjx​Sj+1x{\cal H}^{\prime}=\delta\sum_{j}S^{x}_{j}S^{x}_{j+1}. In these cases, [Sx,ℋ′]=0[S^{x},{\cal H}^{\prime}]=0 holds, and consequently

d​Sxd​t=H​Sy.\frac{dS^{x}}{dt}=HS^{y}. (16)

This identity leads to

χx​x′′​(0,ω)=H2ω2​χy​y′′​(0,ω),\chi^{\prime\prime}_{xx}(0,\omega)=\frac{H^{2}}{\omega^{2}}\chi^{\prime\prime}_{yy}(0,\omega), (17)

and more generally, for the polarization in the direction α\alpha in the x​yxy-plane,

χα​α​(0,ω)=H2​cos2⁡Φ+ω2​sin2⁡Φω2​χy​y​(0,ω),\chi^{\alpha\alpha}(0,\omega)=\frac{H^{2}\cos^{2}{\Phi}+\omega^{2}\sin^{2}{\Phi}}{\omega^{2}}\chi^{yy}(0,\omega), (18)

where Φ\Phi is the angle between xx and α\alpha. (In the notation of Refs. 15, 16, 17, θ=90\theta=90 degree and their ϕ\phi corresponds to our Φ\Phi.)

For a sharp resonance concentrated near ω∼H\omega\sim H, the polarization dependence is not significant. However, if the center of the resonance is defined by the average frequency of the spectrum

ω¯α=∫ω​Iα​(ω)​𝑑ω∫Iα​(ω)​𝑑ω,\bar{\omega}_{\alpha}=\frac{\int\omega I_{\alpha}(\omega)d\omega}{\int I_{\alpha}(\omega)d\omega}, (19)

ω¯x<ω¯y\bar{\omega}_{x}<\bar{\omega}_{y} because the higher frequency part is emphasized in the latter. As a consequence, there is a positive frequency shift for the polarization in yy axis, compared to the case where in xx axis.

This is in agreement with theoretical and experimental results in Refs. 15, 16 and numerical results in Ref. 14, on the exchange anisotropy. We note that, in the actual experiments on ESR, the resonance frequency is kept fixed and the applied field is scanned to measure the absorption. Because of this, it is customary to discuss the shift of the resonance field for a fixed frequency. The direction (positive or negative) of the field shift is opposite to that of the frequency shift we discuss in this paper. They find that the resonance field is shifted negatively for the polarization in yy direction compared to the xx polarization case, which is indeed consistent with our result. The angular dependence is also consistent with the theoretical formula in Ref. 15. On the other hand, in Ref. 17, the polarization dependence is studied by a different formalism (Mori’s memory function method.) When the anisotropy axis is perpendicular to the applied field, the obtained polarization dependence is rather opposite to the above, and is in contradiction to our rigorous result (17).

III Field-theory approach to the S=1/2S=1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain

III.1 Bosonization of S=1/2S=1/2 Heisenberg chain

In the present paper, we mainly discuss ESR on the one-dimensional S=1/2S=1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet

ℋ0=J​∑jS→j⋅S→j+1.{\cal H}_{0}=J\sum_{j}\vec{S}_{j}\cdot\vec{S}_{j+1}. (20)

with symmetry-breaking perturbation ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime} and of course the Zeeman term ℋZ{\cal H}_{Z}. The low-energy physics of the one-dimensional quantum antiferromagnets is well described by field theory methods (bosonization). In this section, we briefly summarize the aspects of this approach that are relevant to the present discussion of the ESR. We refer the reader to Refs. 18, 19 for more details. While the method is now standard, here we also clarify subtleties specific to ESR problems, which are related to the weakly broken S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry discussed in Section II.

The effective field theory of the S=1/2S=1/2 Heisenberg chain ℋ0{\cal H}_{0} is given by the free boson Lagrangian

ℒ=12​[(∂0ϕ)2−(∂1ϕ)2],{\cal L}=\frac{1}{2}\left[(\partial_{0}\phi)^{2}-(\partial_{1}\phi)^{2}\right], (21)

where x0=v​tx^{0}=vt, x1=xx^{1}=x and we make identification ϕ∼ϕ+2​π​R\phi\sim\phi+2\pi R with the compactification radius RR. The radius RR is actually fixed to the value 1/2​π1/\sqrt{2\pi} by the S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry. Hereafter we set v=1v=1 for simplicity; the spinon velocity vv can be recovered by dimensional analysis when necessary.

At zero uniform field, the spin operators may be written in terms of the field ϕ\phi as follows:

Sjz\displaystyle S^{z}_{j} ∼\displaystyle\sim 12​π​R​∂ϕ∂x+Csz​(−1)j​cos⁡ϕR\displaystyle\frac{1}{2\pi R}\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial x}+C_{s}^{z}(-1)^{j}\cos{\frac{\phi}{R}} (22)
Sj−\displaystyle S^{-}_{j} ∼\displaystyle\sim Cu−​e−i​2​π​R​ϕ~​cos⁡ϕR+Cs−​(−1)j​e−i​2​π​R​ϕ~,\displaystyle C_{u}^{-}e^{-i2\pi R\tilde{\phi}}\cos{\frac{\phi}{R}}+C^{-}_{s}(-1)^{j}e^{-i2\pi R\tilde{\phi}}, (23)

where the dual field ϕ~\tilde{\phi} is defined in terms of right-mover φR\varphi_{R} and φL\varphi_{L} as ϕ=φR+φL\phi=\varphi_{R}+\varphi_{L} and ϕ~=φR−φL\tilde{\phi}=\varphi_{R}-\varphi_{L}. While SzS^{z} and Sx,yS^{x,y} are represented in a very different way, their correlation functions turn out to be equal at the S​U​(2)SU(2) invariant radius R=1/2​πR=1/\sqrt{2\pi}, as required from the symmetry of the original Heisenberg chain.

The dynamical structure factor 𝒮α​α{\cal S}^{\alpha\alpha} (Fourier transformation of the spin correlation function) of the Heisenberg chain has been studied in detail. It is equivalent to the dynamical susceptibility for T=0T=0 and ω>0\omega>0. At zero temperature, the dynamical structure factor is non-vanishing only in the limited region of the frequency ω\omega – momentum qq space shown in Fig. 1. The field theory actually can handle only the low-energy excitations near momentum 00 and π\pi. The structure factor for 𝒮z​z{\cal S}^{zz} near q=0q=0 and q=πq=\pi is given by the correlation function of ∂ϕ/∂x\partial\phi/\partial x and cos⁡(ϕ/R)\cos{(\phi/R)} respectively. At T=0T=0, they read

𝒮z​z​(ω,q)∝δ⁡(ω−|q|)​θ​(ω){\cal S}^{zz}(\omega,q)\propto\delta(\omega-|q|)\theta(\omega) (24)

for q∼0q\sim 0 and

𝒮z​z​(ω,q)∝1ω2−(q−π)2​θ​(ω−|q−π|){\cal S}^{zz}(\omega,q)\propto\frac{1}{\sqrt{\omega^{2}-(q-\pi)^{2}}}\theta(\omega-|q-\pi|) (25)

for q∼πq\sim\pi. It is noted that the structure factor is completely sharp and is delta-function like at q∼0q\sim 0. In fact, the structure factor at q∼0q\sim 0 remains so even at finite temperature. As mentioned before, the structure factor is of course isotropic (𝒮x​x=𝒮y​y=𝒮z​z{\cal S}^{xx}={\cal S}^{yy}={\cal S}^{zz}) at H=0H=0 for the isotropic Heisenberg chain.

Now let us consider the effect of the applied magnetic field. The Zeeman term ℋZ{\cal H}_{Z} in the Lagrangian becomes, upon bosonization,

ℒH=H2​π​∂ϕ∂x.{\cal L}_{H}={H\over\sqrt{2\pi}}{\partial\phi\over\partial x}. (26)

This term can be eliminated by a redefinition of the boson field

ϕ⁡(t,x)→ϕ⁡(t,x)+H2​π​x.\phi(t,x)\to\phi(t,x)+{H\over\sqrt{2\pi}}x. (27)

but ϕ~\tilde{\phi} remains unchanged. This is equivalent to the shift of chiral fields as

φR→φR+12​2​π​H​x,φL→φL+12​2​π​H​x.\varphi_{R}\rightarrow\varphi_{R}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\pi}}Hx,\varphi_{L}\rightarrow\varphi_{L}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\pi}}Hx. (28)

While this leaves the free Lagrangian unchanged, it does change the bosonization formulae of physical spin operators:

Sz\displaystyle S^{z} ∼\displaystyle\sim m+12​π​R​∂ϕ∂x+Csz​cos⁡[ϕR+(H+π)​x],\displaystyle m+\frac{1}{2\pi R}\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial x}+C_{s}^{z}\cos{[\frac{\phi}{R}+(H+\pi)x]}, (29)
S±\displaystyle S^{\pm} ∼\displaystyle\sim Cu−​e−i​2​π​ϕ~​cos⁡(ϕR+H​x)+Cs−​(−1)j​e−i​2​π​R​ϕ~.\displaystyle C_{u}^{-}e^{-i\sqrt{2\pi}\tilde{\phi}}\cos{(\frac{\phi}{R}+Hx)}+C^{-}_{s}(-1)^{j}e^{-i2\pi R\tilde{\phi}}. (30)

The first term mm in SzS^{z} represents the expectation value of the magnetization induced by the magnetic field HH. For a small magnetic field, mm is proportional to the field HH. Another important feature is that the applied field induces the shift of the soft-mode momentum[20, 21]. The shift occur differently for the longitudinal (zz) and the transverse (x,yx,y) components. The gapless points under the applied uniform field HH are at q=0q=0 (uniform part) and q=π±Hq=\pi\pm H (“staggered” part) for the longitudinal modes. For the transverse modes, they are at q=±Hq=\pm H (“uniform” part) and q=πq=\pi (staggered part.)

Let us focus on the transverse mode near q=0q=0, because the transverse mode at q=0q=0 is measured in ESR in the Faraday configuration. For simplicity, here we restrict ourselves to zero temperature. In the low energy effective theory, the “uniform” part of the S±S^{\pm} is given

S±∝e±(i​H​x+i​8​π​ϕR)+e∓(i​H​x+i​8​π​ϕL),S^{\pm}\propto e^{\pm(iHx+i\sqrt{8\pi}\phi_{R})}+e^{\mp(iHx+i\sqrt{8\pi}\phi_{L})}, (31)

where we have used the S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetric compactification radius R=1/2​πR=1/\sqrt{2\pi} (see below for reason for taking this value.) This gives the correlation function of S±S^{\pm} at zero temperature:

⟨S+​(t,x)​S−​(0,0)⟩∝ei​H​x(t−i​ϵ+x)2+e−i​H​x(t−i​ϵ−x)2\langle S^{+}(t,x)S^{-}(0,0)\rangle\propto{e^{iHx}\over(t-i\epsilon+x)^{2}}+{e^{-iHx}\over(t-i\epsilon-x)^{2}} (32)

Dynamical structure factor S+⁣−S_{+-}, which is the Fourier transform of the above is,

S+⁣−​(ω,q)\displaystyle S_{+-}(\omega,q) ∝\displaystyle\propto ∫−∞∞d​t​∫−∞∞d​x​ei⁡(ω​t−q​x)​[ei​H​x(t−i​ϵ+x)2+e−i​H​x(t−i​ϵ−x)2]\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dxe^{i(\omega t-qx)}\left[{e^{iHx}\over(t-i\epsilon+x)^{2}}+{e^{-iHx}\over(t-i\epsilon-x)^{2}}\right] (33)
=\displaystyle= ∫−∞∞d​x​[−2​π​ω​θ​(ω)]​e−i​q​x​[ei​H​x−i​ω​x+e−i​H​x+i​ω​x]\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx[-2\pi\omega\theta(\omega)]e^{-iqx}\left[e^{iHx-i\omega x}+e^{-iHx+i\omega x}\right]
∝\displaystyle\propto ω​θ​(ω)​[δ⁡(ω−H+q)+δ⁡(ω−H−q)].\displaystyle\omega\theta(\omega)[\delta(\omega-H+q)+\delta(\omega-H-q)].

The other one S−⁣+S_{-+} is given by replacing H→−HH\rightarrow-H in the above, using the time reversal transformation. Thus

S−⁣+​(ω,q)∝ω​θ​(ω)​[δ⁡(ω+H+q)+δ⁡(ω+H−q)].S_{-+}(\omega,q)\propto\omega\theta(\omega)[\delta(\omega+H+q)+\delta(\omega+H-q)]. (34)

Namely, S+⁣−S_{+-} and S−⁣+S_{-+} give different branches of excitation. The fact that S−⁣+S_{-+} does not contain the branch (33) was recognized earlier (see Fig. 17 of Ref. 21.) On the other hand, that S+⁣−S_{+-} lacks the branch (34) (at least in the low-energy limit) was apparently not appreciated in Fig. 18 of Ref. 21. Sx​xS_{xx} and Sy​yS_{yy} are given by their superposition

Sx​x​(ω,q)=Sy​y​(ω,q)∝ω⁡[δ⁡(ω−|q+H|)+δ⁡(ω−|q−H|)].S_{xx}(\omega,q)=S_{yy}(\omega,q)\propto\omega[\delta(\omega-|q+H|)+\delta(\omega-|q-H|)]. (35)

This zero-temperature transverse structure factor near q=0q=0 under the applied magnetic field is shown in Fig. 2. Because the structure factor near q=0q=0 was sharp, and the gapless point is shifted by HH, we expect a sharp resonance at energy ω∼H\omega\sim H at q=0q=0. This corresponds to the expected paramagnetic ESR for the isotropic Heisenberg chain.

However, it should be noted that we have so far ignored various renormalization effects due to the applied magnetic field. There are irrelevant operators, which themselves vanish in the low-energy limit but renormalize parameters of the low-energy effective theory. The way they renormalize is affected by the applied magnetic field. In general, the precise value of the momentum shift is given by 2​π​m2\pi m rather than HH, where mm is the magnetization. This can be derived from the shift of Fermi momentum in the Jordan-Wigner transformation, and also is required from a rigorous version of Luttinger’s theorem in one dimension[22]. Restoring the spinon velocity vv, the ESR frequency appears to be given by 2​π​m​v2\pi mv. For the standard Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain in an applied field, the magnetization mm and the spinon velocity vv can be obtained as a function of HH from the Bethe Ansatz integral equation. Generally, 2​π​m​v2\pi mv is different from HH except in the zero field limit, implying that the ESR frequency deviates from HH. However, this cannot be true, because the equation of motion for the original Heisenberg model (under an applied field) requires the resonance to be exactly at the frequency HH. The resolution is that, the dispersion relation for q∼0q\sim 0 is not completely linear. The curvature of the dispersion comes form irrelevant operators which break Lorentz invariance. Because of the curvature, the resonance frequency at q=0q=0 is modified from 2​π​m​v2\pi mv, which is derived assuming the linear dispersion. What the equation of motion tells us is that these renormalization effects miraculously cancel, to give the resonance exactly at ω=H\omega=H for q=0q=0. With this nontrivial mechanism in mind, we will take the momentum shift as HH, setting the spinon velocity v=1v=1.

There is another “miraculous” cancellation similar to the above. At zero field, the compactification radius of the effective field theory is fixed to the special S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetric value R=1/2​πR=1/\sqrt{2\pi}, as is required from the S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry of the original Heisenberg model. However, in the presence of the applied field, the S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry is of course broken down to U⁡(1)U(1). Correspondingly, the radius RR is renormalized away from the S​U​(2)SU(2) point by the applied field. The renormalized radius RR as a function of the applied field HH has been also obtained from the exact Bethe Ansatz solution [23]. It is indeed rather sensitive to HH for small H/JH/J. A consequence of the radius renormalization is the dependence of the correlation exponents on the applied field. In particular, the “uniform” part of the transverse spin operator, which is relevant for ESR, is represented by the vertex operator of the type exp⁡[±2​π​i​R​ϕ~±ϕ/R]\exp{[\pm 2\pi iR\tilde{\phi}\pm\phi/R]}; its conformal weight is given by

(Δ,Δ¯)=(1+Δ′,Δ′)(\Delta,\bar{\Delta})=(1+\Delta^{\prime},\Delta^{\prime}) (36)

or (Δ′,1+Δ′)(\Delta^{\prime},1+\Delta^{\prime}), where

Δ′=(2​π​R−1/R)28​π,\Delta^{\prime}=\frac{(2\pi R-1/R)^{2}}{8\pi}, (37)

which does depend on RR. As a result, the structure factor is no longer given by a delta-function for R≠1/2​πR\neq 1/\sqrt{2\pi}. More explicitly, the retarded Green’s function of a conformal primary field with conformal weight (Δ,Δ¯)(\Delta,\bar{\Delta}) at finite temperature TT is obtained explicitly [24] as

G(Δ,Δ¯)R​(ω,q)=−sin⁡(2​π​Δ)​(2​π​T)2​(Δ+Δ¯−1)​B​(Δ−i​ω+q4​π​T,1−2​Δ)​B​(Δ¯−i​ω−q4​π​T,1−2​Δ¯),G^{R}_{(\Delta,\bar{\Delta})}(\omega,q)=-\sin{(2\pi\Delta)}(2\pi T)^{2(\Delta+\bar{\Delta}-1)}B(\Delta-i\frac{\omega+q}{4\pi T},1-2\Delta)B(\bar{\Delta}-i\frac{\omega-q}{4\pi T},1-2\bar{\Delta}), (38)

where BB denotes the Euler Beta function:

B⁡(x,y)=Γ⁡(x)​Γ​(y)Γ⁡(x+y)B(x,y)={\Gamma(x)\Gamma(y)\over\Gamma(x+y)} (39)

and Γ\Gamma is Euler’s Gamma function. Considering the momentum shift induced by the applied field, the absorption measured in ESR corresponds to the Green’s function evaluated at q=Hq=H. Thus, the spectrum is given by the delta function only if (Δ,Δ¯)=(1,0)(\Delta,\bar{\Delta})=(1,0) or (0,1)(0,1), namely R=1/2​πR=1/\sqrt{2\pi}. The renormalization of RR due to the applied field seems to imply that the ESR spectrum should not be given by a delta-function, even in the absence of the perturbation ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime}.

However, this is inconsistent with the equation of motion of the original Heisenberg model. It predicts a completely sharp (delta-function) resonance precisely at the Zeeman energy even for a finite field HH. Since the equation of motion is exact and rigorous for the original spin problem, we conclude that we should take the unrenormalized, S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetric value R=1/2​πR=1/\sqrt{2\pi} even in a finite field, for the calculation of the ESR. This appears contradictory to the well-established renormalization of RR due to the applied field. This is not a real contradiction, however, because the standard result on the renormalization of the radius is determined at the zero energy limit, while the ESR probes the excitation at the finite energy HH. In general, effective coupling constants depend on the energy scale as a consequence of the renormalization. We may introduce an effective radius R⁡(ω)R(\omega) as a function of the energy scale ω\omega. While the determination of the function R⁡(ω)R(\omega) in general is a tedious task, the exact equation of motion on ESR gives the restriction at the Zeeman energy: R⁡(ω=H)=1/2​πR(\omega=H)=1/\sqrt{2\pi}. The non-renormalization could be related to the qualitative understanding of the RG flow in the presence of the applied field, Fig. 7 in Ref. 7. The RG flow in the presence of the applied field is almost identical to that in the zero field, down to energy scale of O⁡(H)O(H), where the flow is “cut off.” If we look at the energy HH, the effective theory may be almost identical to the isotropic one. This argument would not, however, explain why the effective radius should be exactly at the S​U​(2)SU(2) point. From the viewpoint of the field theory, this is again a miraculous cancellation between the renormalization by the uniform field and that by the finite energy. The equation of motion, although quite simple, gives an exact and highly nontrivial constraint on the effective field theory description.

Thus, in the following calculations we do not include the radius renormalization due to the applied field, and take the S​U​(2)SU(2)-symmetric value R=1/2​πR=1/\sqrt{2\pi}. As a result, the appropriate effective field theory of ESR is an S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetric one, namely the level-1 S​U​(2)SU(2) Wess-Zumino-Witten (WZW) theory, even in a finite field; all the effects of the applied field are represented by the shift of the ϕ\phi field (27), resulting in the momentum shift (29) and (30). This may be regarded as a field theory representation of the crucial S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry which is broken only weakly, discussed in Section II.

It is often convenient to introduce the operators in non-Abelian bosonization to make the symmetry manifest. S​U​(2)SU(2) current operators JαJ^{\alpha} (α=x,y,z\alpha=x,y,z) are related to the Abelian bosonization as follows:

JRz​(w)\displaystyle J^{z}_{R}(w) =\displaystyle= i​4​π​∂φR​(w),\displaystyle i\sqrt{4\pi}\partial\varphi_{R}(w), (40)
JR±​(w)\displaystyle J^{\pm}_{R}(w) =\displaystyle= 2​e±i​8​π​φR​(w),\displaystyle\sqrt{2}e^{\pm i\sqrt{8\pi}\varphi_{R}(w)}, (41)
JLz​(w¯)\displaystyle J^{z}_{L}(\bar{w}) =\displaystyle= −i​4​π​∂¯​φL​(w¯),\displaystyle-i\sqrt{4\pi}\bar{\partial}\varphi_{L}(\bar{w}), (42)
JL±​(w¯)\displaystyle J^{\pm}_{L}(\bar{w}) =\displaystyle= 2​e∓i​8​π​φL​(w¯),\displaystyle\sqrt{2}e^{\mp i\sqrt{8\pi}\varphi_{L}(\bar{w})}, (43)

where J±=Jx±i​JyJ^{\pm}=J^{x}\pm iJ^{y}, we have introduced complex coordinates w=τ+i​xw=\tau+ix (τ=i​t\tau=it) and ϕ⁡(w,w¯)=φ⁡(w)+φ¯​(w¯)\phi(w,\bar{w})=\varphi(w)+\bar{\varphi}(\bar{w}). JR⁡(L)αJ^{\alpha}_{R(L)} is the right-mover (left-mover) component of the current, and we have normalized them by

⟨JRa​(w1)​JRb​(w2)⟩=δa​b(w1−w2)2,\langle J^{a}_{R}(w_{1})J^{b}_{R}(w_{2})\rangle=\frac{\delta^{ab}}{(w_{1}-w_{2})^{2}}, (44)

where a,b=x,y,za,b=x,y,z and the complex coordinate w=τ+i​x=−i⁡(t−x)w=\tau+ix=-i(t-x) and likewise for the LL sector. (We note that this is different normalization from Ref. 25.)

The “uniform” part of the spin operators SαS^{\alpha} correspond to the S​U​(2)SU(2) currents JαJ^{\alpha}, while the “staggered” part is related to the S​U​(2)SU(2) triplet nα=Tr​g​σαn^{\alpha}={\rm Tr}{g\sigma^{\alpha}} where the S​U​(2)SU(2) matrix field gβα​(x,t)g^{\alpha}_{\beta}(x,t) is the fundamental field of the Wess-Zumino-Witten non-linear σ\sigma-model. Eqs. (29) and (30) may be rewritten as

Sz\displaystyle S^{z} ∼\displaystyle\sim 18​π2​(JRz+JLz)+Cs​[cos⁡(H+π)​x​nz+sin⁡(H+π)​x​tr​g],\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{8\pi^{2}}}(J^{z}_{R}+J^{z}_{L})+C_{s}\left[\cos{(H+\pi)x}n^{z}+\sin{(H+\pi)x}{\rm tr}g\right], (45)
S±\displaystyle S^{\pm} ∼\displaystyle\sim 18​π2​(JR±​e±i​H​x+JL−​e∓i​H​x).+(−1)x​Cs​n±,\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{8\pi^{2}}}(J^{\pm}_{R}e^{\pm iHx}+J^{-}_{L}e^{\mp iHx}).+(-1)^{x}C_{s}n^{\pm}, (46)

The “staggered” part of SzS^{z} may be written as (−1)x​nz(-1)^{x}n^{z} at H=0H=0, but is a mixture of nzn^{z} and tr​g{\rm tr}g in a finite field.

The ESR absorption intensity is related to the Green’s function of Sx,yS^{x,y}; thus what is needed in the field theory is the Green’s function of Jx,yJ^{x,y} at momentum ±H\pm H.

III.2 Perturbations

Having established the effective field theory for the unperturbed system ℋ0+ℋZ{\cal H}_{0}+{\cal H}_{Z}, we now want to calculate the effects of the perturbation ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime} on the ESR lineshape. Assuming that the perturbation ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime} is small, ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime} can be mapped to an operator of the level-1 S​U​(2)SU(2) WZW theory.

In principle, an infinite variety of symmetry breaking perturbations ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime} is possible. In fact, there are infinitely many operators also in the field theory. However, most of the operators have large scaling dimensions, and thus renormalize rapidly to zero under the RG transformation. Thus, at low enough temperatures, only a few types of perturbations with smaller scaling dimensions are important.

The operators with the lowest scaling dimension 1/21/2 are nαn^{\alpha} and tr​g{\rm tr}g in WZW theory. In the original spin chain Hamiltonian (at H=0H=0), they correspond to the staggered field (3 independent perturbations corresponding to three directions) and the bond alternation. However, the bond-alternation does not break the S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry and hence should not affect the ESR lineshape, although it is not trivial to see this in the field theory. On the other hand, the staggered field perturbation does break the S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry and thus affects the ESR lineshape. The operators of interest with the second lowest scaling dimension 22, which are marginal, are JLα​JRαJ^{\alpha}_{L}J^{\alpha}_{R}. They correspond to the exchange anisotropy in the spin chain Hamiltonian. We will discuss these two most important cases in later sections.

While we use the S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetric field theory, care should be taken with the momentum shift due to the applied field. The momentum shift is determined by a simple rule in Abelian bosonization formulation (28). Namely, if one writes some operator at zero field in terms of φ\varphi’s, the above replacement gives a correct formula under the finite field HH. The operator corresponding to the perturbation ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime} may contain an oscillating factor. While such a term may be ignored in order to know whether there is a finite excitation gap above the ground state, it should be retained in theory of ESR which probes finite momentum of the effective field theory. For a general perturbation, the oscillating factor appears in the effective field theory, and it makes the theoretical analysis rather complicated. In this paper, we focus on a few simple cases in which there is no oscillating term (with finite momentum) in the effective Lagrangian. This still includes several cases of physical interest which are mentioned below.

III.2.1 Transverse staggered field

A quasi one-dimensional spin system often has an alternating crystal structure along the chain. In such a case, generally we expect two features which are absent in a uniform system.

staggered gg-tensor

The magnetic field H→\vec{H} couples to the spin as μB​∑j,a,bHa​[ga​bu+(−1)j​ga​bs]​Sjb\mu_{B}\sum_{j,a,b}H^{a}[g^{u}_{ab}+(-1)^{j}g^{s}_{ab}]S^{b}_{j}, where gsg^{s} is the staggered component of the gg-tensor.

Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction

The low symmetry allows the antisymmetric interaction[26, 27] ∑jD→j⋅(S→j×S→j+1)\sum_{j}\vec{D}_{j}\cdot(\vec{S}_{j}\times\vec{S}_{j+1}) .

The DM interaction can be either uniform (D→j=D→\vec{D}_{j}=\vec{D}) or staggered (D→j=(−1)j​D→\vec{D}_{j}=(-1)^{j}\vec{D}.)

When the staggered gg-tensor is present, an effective staggered field ∝gs​H→\propto g^{s}\vec{H} is produced upon an application of the external field. The direction of the staggered field is often approximately perpendicular to the applied field, although it is not necessarily so. The effect of the DM interaction is less trivial, but it can be actually eliminated by an exact transformation. Let us consider the case of a staggered DM interaction, and choose the axes so that the DM vector D→\vec{D} is parallel to the zz-axis. Then the Hamiltonian including the DM interaction is given by

ℋD​M\displaystyle{\cal H}_{DM} =\displaystyle= J​∑jS→j⋅S→j+1+(−1)j​D​(Sjx​Sj+1y−Sjy​Sj+1x)\displaystyle J\sum_{j}\vec{S}_{j}\cdot\vec{S}_{j+1}+(-1)^{j}D(S^{x}_{j}S^{y}_{j+1}-S^{y}_{j}S^{x}_{j+1}) (47)
=\displaystyle= 12​∑j[𝒥​S2​j−1+​S2​j−+𝒥∗​S2​j+​S2​j+1−+(h.c.)]\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j}[{\cal J}S^{+}_{2j-1}S^{-}_{2j}+{\cal J}^{*}S^{+}_{2j}S^{-}_{2j+1}+(\mbox{h.c.})]
+J∑j[S2​j−1zS2​jz+S2​jzS2​j+1z],\displaystyle+J\sum_{j}[S^{z}_{2j-1}S^{z}_{2j}+S^{z}_{2j}S^{z}_{2j+1}],

where 𝒥≡J+i​D{\cal J}\equiv J+iD. Now let us define the angle α=tan−1⁡D/J\alpha=\tan^{-1}{D/J}, and rotate the spin at site jj by the angle (−1)j​α/2(-1)^{j}\alpha/2 about zz axis:

Sj+→Sj+​ei​(−1)j​α/2S^{+}_{j}\rightarrow S^{+}_{j}e^{i(-1)^{j}\alpha/2} (48)

Then we obtain the Hamiltonian of the XXZ chain

H^=∑j[JSjzSj+1z+|𝒥|2(Sj+Sj+1−+h.c.)].\hat{H}=\sum_{j}[JS_{j}^{z}S_{j+1}^{z}+\frac{|{\cal J}|}{2}(S_{j}^{+}S_{j+1}^{-}+h.c.)]. (49)

It is argued[28] that this anisotropic exchange can cancel the pre-existing one.

Now suppose that an external field HH is applied in xx direction. The applied field is transformed as

−H∑jSjx→−H∑j[cosα2Sjx+(−1)jsinα2Sjy].-H\sum_{j}S^{x}_{j}\to-H\sum_{j}[\cos{\frac{\alpha}{2}}S^{x}_{j}+(-1)^{j}\sin{\frac{\alpha}{2}}S^{y}_{j}]. (50)

by the above transformation. Thus, in the presence of the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, the applied uniform field produces an effective staggered field[6]. For general orientations of D→\vec{D} of the staggered DM interaction

ℋD​M=∑j(−1)j​D→⋅(S→j×S→j+1),{\cal H}_{DM}=\sum_{j}(-1)^{j}\vec{D}\cdot(\vec{S}_{j}\times\vec{S}_{j+1}), (51)

the effective staggered field due to the DM interaction is given by D→×H→/(2​J)\vec{D}\times\vec{H}/(2J)

These two effects give an effective transverse staggered field which is approximately perpendicular to the applied field. This mechanism is important in studying properties of several quasi-one dimensional antiferromagnets including Cu benzoate[5, 6, 7], Yb4As3[8] and Pyrimidine Cu dinitrate[9].

III.2.2 Exchange Anisotropy

The exchange anisotropy is the second relevant perturbation which affects the ESR lineshape. The dipolar interaction which exists in any real magnetic system is given by, restoring the Bohr magneton μB\mu_{B},

Hd​p=(g​μB)2​∑i​j[S→i⋅S→j|r→i​j|3−3​(S→i⋅r→i​j)​(S→j⋅r→i​j)|r→i​j|5],H_{dp}=(g\mu_{B})^{2}\sum_{ij}\left[\frac{\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{j}}{|\vec{r}_{ij}|^{3}}-\frac{3(\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{r}_{ij})(\vec{S}_{j}\cdot\vec{r}_{ij})}{|\vec{r}_{ij}|^{5}}\right], (52)

where r→i​j\vec{r}_{ij} represents the vector from site ii and jj and for the simplicity the gg-factor is assumed to be uniform and isotropic. In a spin chain, the vector r→i​j\vec{r}_{ij} is parallel to the chain direction, and the dipolar interaction reduces to an effective exchange anisotropy parallel to the chain direction. The effect would be essentially the same with the nearest-neighbor anisotropic exchange interaction, because the dipolar interaction strength decreases rapidly with the distance.

Let us consider the simplest case of the exchange anisotropy

Ha=δ​∑jSjn​Sj+1nH_{a}=\delta\sum_{j}S^{n}_{j}S^{n}_{j+1} (53)

with a symmetry axis nn, which effectively covers the case of the dipolar interaction if nn is taken to be the chain direction. Even in this simple case, a variety of configurations is possible by changing the relative direction of nn and the direction zz of the applied field, as is often done in experiments.

As mentioned before, for a general direction, the perturbation in the field theory is rather complicated, making a calculation from first principles difficult. Thus, in this paper, we will focus on the two simplest cases, namely when n|zn\parallel z and n⟂zn\perp z. The case n|zn\parallel z allows us a direct calculation of the lineshape and will be discussed in Section IV. The latter case n⟂zn\perp z will be discussed in Section VI, based on the self-energy approach developed in Section V.

IV Exchange anisotropy parallel to the field: direct calculation

Here we consider the case where the anisotropy axis is parallel to the applied magnetic field, namely n=zn=z in (53). In this case, it is obvious that there is no polarization dependence as SxS^{x} and SyS^{y} are equivalent.

In this case, the perturbation in the effective field theory is given, at zero magnetic field, as

ℒa=−λ​JRz​JLz,{\cal L}_{a}=-\lambda J^{z}_{R}J^{z}_{L}, (54)

where λ\lambda is a parameter proportional to δ/J\delta/J, for a small anisotropy δ/J\delta/J. The proportionality constant λ​J/δ\lambda J/\delta is non-universal and model-dependent. (For the standard Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain, λ\lambda is determined in Section VI.3 together with a logarithmic correction.)

Before performing an explicit calculation, let us see what can be said about the temperature dependence of the linewidth from a general scaling argument. The perturbation (54) is a marginal one with the scaling dimension 22. Thus, ignoring the logarithmic corrections, scaling arguments imply that the linewidth takes the scaling form

η=T​f​(δJ,HT),\eta=Tf(\frac{\delta}{J},\frac{H}{T}), (55)

where we have used the fact that η\eta has the dimension of energy. In fact, this scaling argument can be applied to any direction of the applied field. On the other hand, the explicit form of the scaling function ff cannot be determined by the scaling argument alone.

Now let us calculate the linewidth explicitly for the anisotropy parallel to the applied field. As we have discussed, all the effect of the applied uniform field is represented by the shift of the ϕ\phi field (27). Consequently, the perturbation under the applied field HH is

ℒa=−λ​JRz​JLz−λ​H2​(JRz+JLz)−λ​H22.{\cal L}_{a}=-\lambda J^{z}_{R}J^{z}_{L}-\frac{\lambda H}{\sqrt{2}}(J^{z}_{R}+J^{z}_{L})-\frac{\lambda H^{2}}{2}. (56)

The third term is a constant and thus can be ignored. The second term is

−λ​H2​(JRz+JLz)=−2​π​λ​H​12​π​∂ϕ∂x,-\frac{\lambda H}{\sqrt{2}}(J^{z}_{R}+J^{z}_{L})=-2\pi\lambda H\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial x}, (57)

which is equivalent to the additional magnetic field of −2​π​λ​H-2\pi\lambda H. This can be absorbed by a renormalization of the magnetic field, giving the shift of the resonance by −2​π​λ​H-2\pi\lambda H. This shift is first order in the perturbation δ\delta and the field HH.

Now, let us discuss the effect of the first term. We should calculate the correlation function ⟨J+​J−⟩\langle J^{+}J^{-}\rangle in the presence of the perturbation −λ​JRz​JLz-\lambda J^{z}_{R}J^{z}_{L}. For this particular problem, this can be done exactly, because the perturbation JRz​JLzJ^{z}_{R}J^{z}_{L} is proportional to the kinetic term of the free boson Lagrangian; it just gives a renormalization of the compactification radius. That is, the Lagrangian density reads

ℒ\displaystyle{\cal L} =\displaystyle= 12​(∂μϕ)2−λ​JLz​JRz\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{\mu}\phi)^{2}-\lambda J^{z}_{L}J^{z}_{R} (58)
=\displaystyle= 1+2​π​λ2​(∂μϕ)2.\displaystyle\frac{1+2\pi\lambda}{2}(\partial_{\mu}\phi)^{2}.

Rescaling the field ϕ\phi so that the coefficient of the kinetic term is again given by 1/21/2, the renormalized radius RR is given as

R=1+2​π​λ2​π.R=\sqrt{\frac{1+2\pi\lambda}{2\pi}}. (59)

We note that, we have not included the similar renormalization due to the applied field because of the subtleties explained in Section III.1. In contrast, the exchange anisotropy does break the S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry; there is no reason not to include the renormalization in the present case.

The conformal weight of the vertex operator J±=e±i​2​π​R​ϕ~+i​ϕ/RJ^{\pm}=e^{\pm i2\pi R\tilde{\phi}+i\phi/R} is (Δ,Δ¯)=(1+Δ′,Δ′)(\Delta,\bar{\Delta})=(1+\Delta^{\prime},\Delta^{\prime}) or (Δ′,1+Δ′)(\Delta^{\prime},1+\Delta^{\prime}) where Δ′=(2​π​R−1/R)2/(8​π)∼π2​λ2\Delta^{\prime}=(2\pi R-1/R)^{2}/(8\pi)\sim\pi^{2}\lambda^{2}. Its Green’s function at finite temperature is given in eq. (38). As explained, the Green’s function evaluated at the momenta ±H\pm H is relevant for ESR. Near the center of the resonance, the spectrum is dominated by the pole of the Γ\Gamma function; it reduces to

𝒢RS+​S−​(ω)∼const.ω−H+4​π​T​Δ′​i.{{\cal G}^{R}}_{S^{+}S^{-}}(\omega)\sim\frac{\mbox{const.}}{\omega-H+4\pi T\Delta^{\prime}i}. (60)

Thus the resonance is Lorentzian with the width

η=4​π​Δ′​T=4​π3​λ2​T.\eta=4\pi\Delta^{\prime}T=4\pi^{3}\lambda^{2}T. (61)

This is consistent with the scaling argument (55).

To summarize, the exchange anisotropy with the axis parallel to the applied field gives the following effects on paramagnetic ESR.

shift

−2​π​λ​H∝−H​δ-2\pi\lambda H\propto-H\delta

width

4​π3​λ2​T∝(δ/J)2​T4\pi^{3}\lambda^{2}T\propto(\delta/J)^{2}T

V Self-energy approach

In the last Section, the ESR absorption spectrum was calculated directly in the low-energy effective theory. This was made possible because the effective theory reduced to the free boson theory. However, in general, the problem is more difficult because the effective field theory involves interactions.

A possible application of the field theory method to ESR is to evaluate the Green’s function appearing in MK formula (7) by means of the field theory. While the MK formula has been applied to quantum spin chains by several authors, most of the calculations are based on classical or high-temperature approximations which break down at low temperature and in low dimensions. Thus it would be worthwhile to evaluate the MK formula using field theory to study quantum spin systems at lower temperature and in lower dimensions. On the other hand, the crucial assumption of the (single) Lorentzian lineshape is made in using the MK formula usually without a rigorous justification. Moreover, the MK formula ignores the possible polarization dependence discussed in Sec. II.3. Thus, in this section, we develop a new, systematic field-theory approach to ESR, which we call the self-energy approach. The ESR spectrum is given by the imaginary part of the retarded Green’s function of S±S^{\pm}. As we have discussed in the last section, it corresponds to the Green’s function of the current operators in the effective field theory via eq. (46).

We now assume that the perturbation preserves a symmetry which forbids mixing between JxJ^{x} and JyJ^{y}, namely ⟨Jx​Jy⟩=0\langle J^{x}J^{y}\rangle=0. Then the correlation function of the total spin can be decoupled to JxJ^{x} and JyJ^{y} part.

⟨S+​(t)​S−​(0)⟩\displaystyle\langle S^{+}(t)S^{-}(0)\rangle =\displaystyle= 18​π2​∫d​x1​∫d​x2​⟨JRx​(t,x1)​ei​H​(x1−x2)​JRx​(0,x2)⟩+⟨JLx​(t,x1)​e−i​H​(x1−x2)​JLx​(0,x2)⟩\displaystyle\frac{1}{8\pi^{2}}\int dx_{1}\int dx_{2}\langle J^{x}_{R}(t,x_{1})e^{iH(x_{1}-x_{2})}J^{x}_{R}(0,x_{2})\rangle+\langle J^{x}_{L}(t,x_{1})e^{-iH(x_{1}-x_{2})}J^{x}_{L}(0,x_{2})\rangle (62)
+⟨JRx​(t,x1)​ei​H​(x1+x2)​JLx​(0,x2)⟩+⟨JLx​(t,x1)​e−i​H​(x1+x2)​JLx​(0,x2)⟩\displaystyle+\langle J^{x}_{R}(t,x_{1})e^{iH(x_{1}+x_{2})}J^{x}_{L}(0,x_{2})\rangle+\langle J^{x}_{L}(t,x_{1})e^{-iH(x_{1}+x_{2})}J^{x}_{L}(0,x_{2})\rangle
+(Jx→Jy)\displaystyle+(J^{x}\rightarrow J^{y})

Since our effective field theory is S​U​(2)SU(2)-symmetric, we may freely rotate the x​y​zxyz-axes. Thus, instead of calculating correlation functions of JxJ^{x} we can calculate those of JzJ^{z}, with perturbations also rotated correspondingly. The same applies to calculation of JyJ^{y} correlations.

The motivation for us to rotate the x​y​zxyz-axes is that, JzJ^{z} is expressed as a derivative of the boson field ϕ\phi as in eq. (40). Thus the problem is reduced to the calculation of the bosonic correlation function ⟨ϕ​ϕ⟩\langle\phi\phi\rangle. The structure of the bosonic correlation function is well established by the standard diagrammatic perturbation theory, and the ESR lineshape is related to the boson self-energy as we will show below. On the other hand, when the perturbation allows mixing of JxJ^{x} and JyJ^{y} (in the original representation), there seems no way to reduce the problem to the ⟨ϕ​ϕ⟩\langle\phi\phi\rangle correlation function. In such cases, we do not know at present how to construct the theory of ESR based on self-energy. Thus, below we restrict ourselves to the situation in which JxJ^{x} and JyJ^{y} do not mix, in the discussion of the self-energy approach. We remark that there is no apparent difficulty in the application of the MK formula even in cases where the perturbation allows mixing of JxJ^{x} and JyJ^{y}.

As mentioned in Section III.2, we restrict ourselves to the case where the perturbation does not contain an oscillating factor ei​H​xe^{iHx}. Then the contribution from the cross terms such as ⟨JR​JL⟩\langle J_{R}J_{L}\rangle vanish in eq. (62), due to momentum conservation. The correlation function thus reduces, upon Fourier transformation to

⟨S+​S−⟩​(ω)=18​π2​[⟨JRx​JRx⟩​(ω,−H)+⟨JLx​JLx⟩​(ω,H)+⟨JRy​JRy⟩​(ω,−H)+⟨JLy​JLy⟩​(ω,H)]\langle S^{+}S^{-}\rangle(\omega)=\frac{1}{8\pi^{2}}\left[\langle J^{x}_{R}J^{x}_{R}\rangle(\omega,-H)+\langle J^{x}_{L}J^{x}_{L}\rangle(\omega,H)+\langle J^{y}_{R}J^{y}_{R}\rangle(\omega,-H)+\langle J^{y}_{L}J^{y}_{L}\rangle(\omega,H)\right] (63)

where ⟨J​J⟩​(ω,q)\langle JJ\rangle(\omega,q) denotes the correlation function at frequency ω\omega and momentum qq. As we have discussed above, we now rotate the axes and calculate JzJ^{z} correlation function instead of JxJ^{x} and JyJ^{y}, to obtain

⟨S+​S−⟩​(ω)=\displaystyle\langle S^{+}S^{-}\rangle(\omega)= (64)
18​π2​[⟨JRz​JRz⟩x→z​(ω,H)+⟨JLz​JLz⟩x→z​(ω,−H)+⟨JRz​JRz⟩y→z​(ω,H)+⟨JLz​JLz⟩y→z​(ω,−H)],\displaystyle\frac{1}{8\pi^{2}}\bigl[\langle J^{z}_{R}J^{z}_{R}\rangle_{x\rightarrow z}(\omega,H)+\langle J^{z}_{L}J^{z}_{L}\rangle_{x\rightarrow z}(\omega,-H)+\langle J^{z}_{R}J^{z}_{R}\rangle_{y\rightarrow z}(\omega,H)+\langle J^{z}_{L}J^{z}_{L}\rangle_{y\rightarrow z}(\omega,-H)\bigr],

where ⟨⟩x→z\langle\rangle_{x\rightarrow z} means the correlation function with the perturbation rotated x→zx\rightarrow z. Using eq. (40) and (42), those correlation functions can be written in terms of bosonic correlation function:

⟨S+​S−⟩​(ω)=(ω+H)24​π​⟨ϕ​ϕ⟩x→z​(ω,H)+(ω+H)24​π​⟨ϕ​ϕ⟩y→z​(ω,H),\langle S^{+}S^{-}\rangle(\omega)=\frac{(\omega+H)^{2}}{4\pi}\langle\phi\phi\rangle_{x\rightarrow z}(\omega,H)+\frac{(\omega+H)^{2}}{4\pi}\langle\phi\phi\rangle_{y\rightarrow z}(\omega,H), (65)

where we have used the symmetry ⟨ϕ​ϕ⟩​(ω,−H)=⟨ϕ​ϕ⟩​(ω,H)\langle\phi\phi\rangle(\omega,-H)=\langle\phi\phi\rangle(\omega,H). The above formula is useful if the perturbation (after the rotation) is given by a Lagrangian density local in the boson field ϕ\phi. If, for example, the Lagrangian density is local in terms of the dual field ϕ~\tilde{\phi} after the rotation y→zy\rightarrow z, the second term in eq. (65) should be replaced by

(ω+H)24​π​⟨ϕ~​ϕ~⟩y→z​(ω,H).\frac{(\omega+H)^{2}}{4\pi}\langle\tilde{\phi}\tilde{\phi}\rangle_{y\rightarrow z}(\omega,H). (66)

In fact, there is a subtlety in defining the current. In the free boson theory without interactions, we have

∂ϕ∂x\displaystyle\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial x} =\displaystyle= ∂ϕ~∂t,\displaystyle\frac{\partial\tilde{\phi}}{\partial t}, (67)
∂ϕ∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial t} =\displaystyle= −∂ϕ~∂x,\displaystyle-\frac{\partial\tilde{\phi}}{\partial x}, (68)

so that we may represent the current operator in terms of either ϕ\phi or ϕ~\tilde{\phi}. However, in the presence of the interaction, we cannot define the dual fields ϕ\phi and ϕ~\tilde{\phi} that satisfy both identities. For example, let us take the Lagrangian density

ℒ=12​(∂μϕ)2−λ​cos⁡β​ϕ,{\cal L}=\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{\mu}\phi)^{2}-\lambda\cos{\beta\phi}, (69)

and define the dual field ϕ~\tilde{\phi} by eq. (67). Then, from the equation of motion, we find

∂xϕ~(t,x)+∂tϕ(t,x)=−βλ∫−∞tcosβϕ(t′,x)dt′,\partial_{x}\tilde{\phi}(t,x)+\partial_{t}\phi(t,x)=-\beta\lambda\int^{t}_{-\infty}\cos{\beta\phi}(t^{\prime},x)dt^{\prime}, (70)

violating eq. (68).

Thus it is not completely clear whether the current operator should be written as a derivative of ϕ\phi or ϕ~\tilde{\phi}. However, upon Fourier transform, the “difference term” (right-hand side of eq. (70)) does not give a sharp peak. (Recall that only the operators of conformal weight (1,0)(1,0) or (0,1)(0,1) produce a delta-function spectrum. Other operators give broad spectrum given by eq. (38), even in the zeroth order.) Moreover, the contribution from the difference term is suppressed by a factor λ2\lambda^{2}. Therefore, the difference term would lead, at most, only to a small and broad background. In discussing the lineshape of the main resonance, we can ignore the difference term and focus on the derivative of either boson field ϕ\phi or ϕ~\tilde{\phi}. For calculational convenience, we choose to use ϕ\phi (or ϕ~\tilde{\phi}) if the interaction is given in terms of ϕ\phi (ϕ~\tilde{\phi}.)

Thus the problem of finding the ESR absorption spectrum is reduced to the calculation of the correlation function of the boson field ϕ\phi. We now make the Wick rotation and consider the corresponding Matsubara Green’s function defined by

𝒢A​B​(τ)=−1Z​Tr​Tτ​[A⁡(τ)​B​(0)],{\cal G}_{AB}(\tau)=-\frac{1}{Z}{\rm Tr}T_{\tau}\left[A(\tau)B(0)\right], (71)

where TτT_{\tau} is the ordering operator with respect to the imaginary time τ\tau, and A⁡(τ)≡eτ​ℋ​A​e−τ​ℋA(\tau)\equiv e^{\tau{\cal H}}Ae^{-\tau{\cal H}}. The standard diagrammatic perturbation theory can be applied to the Matsubara Green’s function. After obtaining the Matsubara Green’s function, we can analytically continue back to real time to obtain the retarded Green’s function.

Provided that the Lagrangian is local in terms of the boson field, its correlation function can be written in a self-energy form:

𝒢ϕ​ϕ​(ωn,q)=−1ωn2+q2+Π⁡(ωn,q),{\cal G}_{\phi\phi}(\omega_{n},q)=\frac{-1}{\omega_{n}^{2}+q^{2}+\Pi(\omega_{n},q)}, (72)

where 𝒢{\cal G} is the (full) Matsubara Green’s function, ωn\omega_{n} is the Matsubara frequency, and Π⁡(ωn,q)\Pi(\omega_{n},q) is the self-energy, namely the sum of all one-particle irreducible diagrams. Thus we obtain

𝒢S+​S−​(ωn,q)∼(i​ωn+H)24​π​−1ωn2+H2+Πx​(ωn,H)+(i​ωn+H)24​π​−1ωn2+H2+Πy​(ωn,H),{\cal G}_{S^{+}S^{-}}(\omega_{n},q)\sim\frac{(i\omega_{n}+H)^{2}}{4\pi}\frac{-1}{\omega_{n}^{2}+H^{2}+\Pi_{x}(\omega_{n},H)}+\frac{(i\omega_{n}+H)^{2}}{4\pi}\frac{-1}{\omega_{n}^{2}+H^{2}+\Pi_{y}(\omega_{n},H)}, (73)

where Πx\Pi_{x} and Πy\Pi_{y} are the self-energy in the Matsubara formalism, respectively for ⟨ϕ​ϕ⟩x→z\langle\phi\phi\rangle_{x\rightarrow z} and ⟨ϕ​ϕ⟩y→z\langle\phi\phi\rangle_{y\rightarrow z}. This gives, upon the analytic continuation, the retarded Green’s function

𝒢S+​S−R​(ω,q)∼(ω+H)24​π​1ω2−H2−ΠxR​(ω,H)+(ω+H)24​π​1ω2−H2−ΠyR​(ω,H),{\cal G}^{R}_{S^{+}S^{-}}(\omega,q)\sim\frac{(\omega+H)^{2}}{4\pi}\frac{1}{\omega^{2}-H^{2}-\Pi^{R}_{x}(\omega,H)}+\frac{(\omega+H)^{2}}{4\pi}\frac{1}{\omega^{2}-H^{2}-\Pi^{R}_{y}(\omega,H)}, (74)

where the “self-energy” ΠαR\Pi^{R}_{\alpha} (α=x,y\alpha=x,y) is defined by the analytic continuation

ΠαR​(i​ωn,q)=Πα​(ωn,q)\Pi^{R}_{\alpha}(i\omega_{n},q)=\Pi_{\alpha}(\omega_{n},q) (75)

for ωn>0\omega_{n}>0.

First let us check what we obtain in the absence of the perturbation. Then ΠxR=ΠyR=0\Pi^{R}_{x}=\Pi^{R}_{y}=0 so that the Green’s function has a pole at ω=H\omega=H:

GS+​S−R​(ω)∼Hπ​1ω−H+i​0.G^{R}_{S^{+}S^{-}}(\omega)\sim\frac{H}{\pi}\frac{1}{\omega-H+i0}. (76)

This means that we have a completely sharp resonance at the Zeeman energy ω=H\omega=H as expected, in agreement with the equation of motion. The residue H/πH/\pi at the pole of the Green’s function gives the intensity of the resonance. This is also consistent with the exact result from the original spin chain.

GS+​S−R(ω)=−i∫0∞dt⟨[S+(t),S−(0)]⟩=2​mω−H+i​0,G^{R}_{S^{+}S^{-}}(\omega)=-i\int_{0}^{\infty}dt\langle[S^{+}(t),S^{-}(0)]\rangle=\frac{2m}{\omega-H+i0}, (77)

where mm is the magnetization. For small field HH, the magnetization is given by m=χu​Hm=\chi_{u}H, where the uniform susceptibility is

χu=12​π\chi_{u}=\frac{1}{2\pi} (78)

in the low-temperature limit, ignoring the effect of the isotropic marginal operator[29]. (We remind the reader that we have been setting v=1v=1.) Thus we obtain the amplitude 2​m=H/π2m=H/\pi, in agreement with eq. (76).

A symmetry breaking perturbation ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime} would give non-vanishing boson self-energy Πx,Πy\Pi_{x},\Pi_{y}. This changes the ESR lineshape. Near the resonance ω∼H\omega\sim H, we can write

𝒢S+​S−R​(ω)=H2​π​1ω−H−12​H​ΠxR​(ω,H)+H2​π​1ω−H−12​H​ΠyR​(ω,H){\cal G}^{R}_{S^{+}S^{-}}(\omega)=\frac{H}{2\pi}\frac{1}{\omega-H-\frac{1}{2H}\Pi^{R}_{x}(\omega,H)}+\frac{H}{2\pi}\frac{1}{\omega-H-\frac{1}{2H}\Pi^{R}_{y}(\omega,H)} (79)

If the self-energy changes smoothly around the resonance ω∼H\omega\sim H, we may regard the self-energy as being constant in a frequency range sufficiently close to the center of resonance. Then, within this range, the lineshape is given by a Lorentzian, and the real and imaginary parts of the self-energy give the shift and width of the ESR, respectively. The linewidth is given by

η=−12​H​Im​ΠαR​(H,H),\eta=\frac{-1}{2H}{\rm Im}{\Pi^{R}_{\alpha}(H,H)}, (80)

while the shift is

Δ​ω=12​H​Re​ΠαR​(H,H),\Delta\omega=\frac{1}{2H}{\rm Re}{\Pi^{R}_{\alpha}(H,H)}, (81)

for α=x,y\alpha=x,y. In general, the signal could be superposition of two Lorentzian spectra corresponding to ΠxR\Pi^{R}_{x} and ΠyR\Pi^{R}_{y}. However, in the concrete cases we study in the present paper, ΠxR\Pi^{R}_{x} and ΠyR\Pi^{R}_{y} are equal; thus a single Lorentzian lineshape is predicted.

Therefore we have successfully formulated the theory of ESR without any particular assumption on the lineshape. The self-energy is usually a smooth function of ω\omega near ω∼H\omega\sim H for finite HH except for the smooth weak background discussed below Eq. (70); we have given a microscopic foundation for the Lorentzian lineshape which is assumed a priori in the MK approach. Application of the present self-energy formalism to two cases relevant to experiments will be discussed in the following sections. However, precisely speaking, our approach is only formulated ignoring the isotropic marginal operator, which is generally present in the effective theory of the Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chains. Some discussions on the effects of the isotropic marginal operator will be given in Section VI.3.

Comparing with the assumption (11) used in our derivation of the MK formula in Appendix A, it is obvious that the MK formula and the self-energy approach are closely related. Namely, Σ\Sigma introduced in eq. (11) corresponds to ΠR/(2​H)\Pi^{R}/(2H) if they vary smoothly around the resonance. The important difference is that it is an assumption that the Green’s function can be written as in eq. (11) with a smooth Σ\Sigma whereas we can prove eq. (72) using the diagrammatic perturbation theory. The self-energy, Π\Pi, is given by the sum of all one-particle irreducible Feynman diagrams as in proven in any book on field theory. In this way, our self-energy formulation effectively gives a proof of the Lorentzian form (11) which is often assumed without a microscopic foundation. We emphasize that, although eq. (11) may appear innocent, it is a rather strong assumption and is far from trivial. When the lineshape turns out to be Lorentzian, the results must agree between the MK and self-energy approaches, if the correlation functions are evaluated correctly. This will be verified for a few cases in Sections VI.2, VIII.2 and VIII.3. On the other hand, while the validity of the MK formula is limited to the lowest order perturbation theory, the self-energy formulation allows us to go beyond that. In fact, we will make a non-perturbative analysis of the lineshape, based on the self-energy formalism, in Section VIII.5.

We note that assumptions similar to eq. (11) have been made in the literature for different problems. Sometimes the (counterpart of) assumed Σ\Sigma in eq. (11) is referred to as the memory function. For example, Giamarchi[30] studied the conductivity of the TL liquid with the bosonization method. His discussion was rather closely related to our analysis of ESR in the present paper. (See also Ref. 32.) In fact, he calculated the ac conductivity of a TL liquid by evaluating the memory function with the field theory. This is quite similar to a field-theory calculation of the MK formula for ESR, which we will discuss in later sections.

We could also apply our self-energy approach to problems such as the conductivity of TL liquids. This might be useful for providing a more rigorous justification and a possibility to go beyond the lowest order perturbation theory. The possible breakdown of the MK formula, in the context of the conductivity of a TL liquid, was discussed by Giamarchi and Millis[31].

VI Exchange anisotropy perpendicular to the magnetic field

Now we consider the exchange anisotropy with the axis perpendicular to the applied magnetic field. Let us take the axis of the anisotropy as the xx-axis. In the low-energy effective theory, at zero uniform field, the anisotropy term is given as

ℒa\displaystyle{\cal L}_{a} =\displaystyle= −λ​JRx​JLx\displaystyle-\lambda J^{x}_{R}J^{x}_{L} (82)
=\displaystyle= −λ2​(JRx​JLx−JRy​JLy)+λ2​JRz​JLz+λ2​J→R⋅J→L.\displaystyle-\frac{\lambda}{2}(J^{x}_{R}J^{x}_{L}-J^{y}_{R}J^{y}_{L})+\frac{\lambda}{2}J^{z}_{R}J^{z}_{L}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\vec{J}_{R}\cdot\vec{J}_{L}.

Here the parameter λ\lambda, which is proportional to δ\delta for a small δ\delta, is the same as the one introduced in eq. (54). The last term J→R⋅J→L\vec{J}_{R}\cdot\vec{J}_{L} of the second line is the isotropic marginal operator, which does not affect the resonance directly and will thus be ignored in the following.

Now let us include the effects (27) of the applied uniform field HH. The first and second terms in eq. (82) are transformed into

ℒa=−λ2​(JRx​JLx−JRy​JLy)+λ2​JRz​JLz+λ​H2​2​(JRz+JLz)+λ​H24.{\cal L}_{a}=-\frac{\lambda}{2}(J^{x}_{R}J^{x}_{L}-J^{y}_{R}J^{y}_{L})+\frac{\lambda}{2}J^{z}_{R}J^{z}_{L}+\frac{\lambda H}{2\sqrt{2}}(J^{z}_{R}+J^{z}_{L})+\frac{\lambda H^{2}}{4}. (83)

Fortunately, there is no oscillating factor ei​H​xe^{iHx} here. The last constant term has no effect in the following, and will be ignored. The third term represents the additional magnetic field of +π​λ​H+\pi\lambda H. (Compare with eq. (56).) This is again absorbed by a renormalization of the uniform field HH, giving the shift of π​λ​H\pi\lambda H.

The remaining problem then is to study the effect of the perturbation

ℒa′=−λ2​(JRx​JLx−JRy​JLy−JRz​JLz){\cal L}^{\prime}_{a}=-\frac{\lambda}{2}(J^{x}_{R}J^{x}_{L}-J^{y}_{R}J^{y}_{L}-J^{z}_{R}J^{z}_{L}) (84)

The first two terms corresponds to an interaction in terms of the boson field ϕ~\tilde{\phi}, and the problem cannot be reduced to a free field theory. Thus it is not possible to calculate the ESR absorption spectrum directly as we have done for the exchange anisotropy parallel to the magnetic field in Section IV. Therefore, we will employ the self-energy approach developed in Section V.

VI.1 Self-energy approach

Because the anisotropy considered here breaks the rotational symmetry in the x​yxy-plane, we expect a polarization dependence. Thus let us consider the correlation function of SxS^{x} and SyS^{y} separately. Under the magnetic field, Sx,yS^{x,y} at zero momentum are expressed as

Sx\displaystyle S^{x} =\displaystyle= JR+​(H)+JL+​(−H)+JR−​(−H)+JL−​(H)2​8​π2,\displaystyle\frac{J^{+}_{R}(H)+J^{+}_{L}(-H)+J^{-}_{R}(-H)+J^{-}_{L}(H)}{2\sqrt{8\pi^{2}}}, (85)
Sy\displaystyle S^{y} =\displaystyle= JR+​(H)+JL+​(−H)−JR−​(−H)−JL−​(H)2​i​8​π2.\displaystyle\frac{J^{+}_{R}(H)+J^{+}_{L}(-H)-J^{-}_{R}(-H)-J^{-}_{L}(H)}{2i\sqrt{8\pi^{2}}}. (86)

JLz​JRz−(JLx​JRx+JLy​JRy)\displaystyle J^{z}_{L}J^{z}_{R}-(J^{x}_{L}J^{x}_{R}+J^{y}_{L}J^{y}_{R}) =\displaystyle= −π​(∂μϕ)2−2​cos⁡8​π​ϕ,\displaystyle-\pi(\partial_{\mu}\phi)^{2}-2\cos{\sqrt{8\pi}\phi}, (90)

The (∂μϕ)2(\partial_{\mu}\phi)^{2} term gives a renormalization of the radius RR. However, in the lowest order of the perturbation theory, its effect is negligible on the boson correlation function ⟨ϕ​ϕ⟩\langle\phi\phi\rangle and thus will be dropped in the following.

Thus, in evaluating ⟨Jz​Jz⟩x\langle J^{z}J^{z}\rangle_{x} we will represent the current operator JzJ^{z} as a derivative of ϕ\phi, so that the problem is reduced to the correlation function of the fundamental boson field ϕ\phi in the presence of the interaction in terms of ϕ\phi. On the other hand, in evaluating ⟨Jz​Jz⟩y\langle J^{z}J^{z}\rangle_{y}, we will express the current JzJ^{z} by of ϕ~\tilde{\phi} for ⟨Jz​Jz⟩y\langle J^{z}J^{z}\rangle_{y}.

As a result, we have

𝒢JRz​JRzRx​(ω,q)\displaystyle{{\cal G}^{R}_{J^{z}_{R}J^{z}_{R}}}^{x}(\omega,q) =\displaystyle= π​(ω−q)2ω2−q2−ΠR​(ω,q),\displaystyle\pi\frac{(\omega-q)^{2}}{\omega^{2}-q^{2}-\Pi^{R}(\omega,q)}, (92)

Plugging these into eqs. (87),(88), we obtain

𝒢x​xR​(ω)\displaystyle{\cal G}^{R}_{xx}(\omega) =\displaystyle= H22​π​1ω2−H2−ΠR​(ω,H),\displaystyle\frac{H^{2}}{2\pi}\frac{1}{\omega^{2}-H^{2}-\Pi^{R}(\omega,H)}, (98)
