where 𝒢α​βR{\cal G}^{R}_{\alpha\beta} is the retarded Green’s functions of the spin operators SαS^{\alpha} and SβS^{\beta}, as defined in eq. (3).

For a direction α\alpha in the x​yxy-plane,

𝒢α​αR=H2​cos2⁡Φ+ω2​sin2⁡Φπ​1ω2−H2−ΠR​(ω,H),{\cal G}^{R}_{\alpha\alpha}=\frac{H^{2}\cos^{2}{\Phi}+\omega^{2}\sin^{2}{\Phi}}{\pi}\frac{1}{\omega^{2}-H^{2}-\Pi^{R}(\omega,H)}, (101)

where Φ\Phi is the angle between xx and α\alpha directions, namely the angle between the anisotropy axis and the polarization of the electromagnetic wave.

As a result, for any directions of the polarization perpendicular to the magnetic field, the ESR lineshape is Lorentzian with the width −ImΠR(H,H)/(2H)-{\rm Im}\Pi^{R}(H,H)/(2H). However, the lineshape has some angle dependence through the numerator H2​cos2⁡θ+ω2​sin2⁡θH^{2}\cos^{2}{\theta}+\omega^{2}\sin^{2}{\theta}. In fact, the present result is consistent with the exact and rigorous relation (18) for original spin model. This serves as a consistency check of our field-theory approach.

Now let us calculate the self-energy Π\Pi of boson field ϕ\phi in the presence of interaction λ​cos⁡8​π​ϕ\lambda\cos{\sqrt{8\pi}\phi}. It is easy to see the first order perturbation to the boson correlation function vanishes due to symmetry. The second order perturbation to the boson correlation function does not vanish and can be calculated by the diagrammatic expansion (ie. Wick’s theorem). The second-order term in the boson correlation function is related to

λ22⋅4​⟨ϕ⁡(1)​ei​8​π​ϕ​(2)​e−i​8​π​ϕ​(3)​ϕ​(4)⟩\displaystyle\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2\cdot 4}\langle\phi(1)e^{i\sqrt{8\pi}\phi(2)}e^{-i\sqrt{8\pi}\phi(3)}\phi(4)\rangle =\displaystyle= λ28∑n,m(i​8​π)nn!(−i​8​π)mm!⟨ϕ(1):ϕn(2)::ϕm(3):ϕ(4)⟩\displaystyle\frac{\lambda^{2}}{8}\sum_{n,m}\frac{(i\sqrt{8\pi})^{n}}{n!}\frac{(-i\sqrt{8\pi})^{m}}{m!}\langle\phi(1):\phi^{n}(2)::\phi^{m}(3):\phi(4)\rangle (102)
=\displaystyle= π​λ2​⟨ϕ⁡(1)​ϕ​(2)⟩​⟨ei​8​π​ϕ​(2)​e−i​8​π​ϕ​(3)⟩​⟨ϕ⁡(3)​ϕ​(4)⟩+(2↔3)\displaystyle\pi\lambda^{2}\langle\phi(1)\phi(2)\rangle\langle e^{i\sqrt{8\pi}\phi(2)}e^{-i\sqrt{8\pi}\phi(3)}\rangle\langle\phi(3)\phi(4)\rangle+(2\leftrightarrow 3)
−π​λ2​⟨ϕ⁡(1)​ϕ​(2)⟩​⟨ei​8​π​ϕ​(2)​e−i​8​π​ϕ​(3)⟩​⟨ϕ⁡(2)​ϕ​(4)⟩+(2↔3)\displaystyle-\pi\lambda^{2}\langle\phi(1)\phi(2)\rangle\langle e^{i\sqrt{8\pi}\phi(2)}e^{-i\sqrt{8\pi}\phi(3)}\rangle\langle\phi(2)\phi(4)\rangle+(2\leftrightarrow 3)
+π​λ2​⟨ϕ⁡(1)​ϕ​(4)⟩​⟨ei​8​π​ϕ​(2)​e−i​8​π​ϕ​(3)⟩\displaystyle+\pi\lambda^{2}\langle\phi(1)\phi(4)\rangle\langle e^{i\sqrt{8\pi}\phi(2)}e^{-i\sqrt{8\pi}\phi(3)}\rangle (103)

The three terms here represent contributions form different kinds of Feynman diagrams, as shown in Fig. 3. The second type of the term −⟨ϕ⁡(1)​ϕ​(2)⟩​⟨ei​8​π​ϕ​(2)​e−i​8​π​ϕ​(3)⟩​⟨ϕ⁡(2)​ϕ​(4)⟩+(2↔3)-\langle\phi(1)\phi(2)\rangle\langle e^{i\sqrt{8\pi}\phi(2)}e^{-i\sqrt{8\pi}\phi(3)}\rangle\langle\phi(2)\phi(4)\rangle+(2\leftrightarrow 3) represents the “tadpole” type Feynman diagram (Fig. 3 (b)), while the last term corresponds to a disconnected Feynman diagram (Fig. 3 (c)), which is canceled by the correction to the partition function.

In fact, there is a similar contribution from e−i​8​π​ϕ​(2)​e+i​8​π​ϕ​(3)e^{-i\sqrt{8\pi}\phi(2)}e^{+i\sqrt{8\pi}\phi(3)} besides the above, and one has to integrate the coordinates 22 and 33 over Euclidean space-time. As a result, we obtain the self-energy in the lowest order (O⁡(λ2)O(\lambda^{2})) of the perturbation as

Π⁡(ωn,q)=4​π​λ2​[G(1,1)​(ωn,q)−G(1,1)​(0,0)],\Pi(\omega_{n},q)=4\pi\lambda^{2}[G_{(1,1)}(\omega_{n},q)-G_{(1,1)}(0,0)], (104)

where G(1,1)G_{(1,1)} is the Matsubara Green’s function of the operator of the conformal weight (1,1)(1,1) in the free boson theory. These two terms come from type (a) and (b) Feynman diagrams in Fig. 3, respectively. Analytic continuation back to real time leads to

ΠR​(ω,q)=4​π​λ2​[G(1,1)R​(ω,q)−G(1,1)R​(0,0)],\Pi^{R}(\omega,q)=4\pi\lambda^{2}[G^{R}_{(1,1)}(\omega,q)-G^{R}_{(1,1)}(0,0)], (105)

where G(1,1)RG^{R}_{(1,1)} is the retarded Green’s function corresponding to the Matsubara Green’s function G(1,1)G_{(1,1)}. Its imaginary part can be derived by taking the limit Δ,Δ¯→1\Delta,\bar{\Delta}\rightarrow 1 in eq. (38):

Im⁡[−G(1,1)R​(ω,q)]=π28​(ω2−q2)​[coth⁡ω+q4​T+coth⁡ω−q4​T].{\rm Im}[-G^{R}_{(1,1)}(\omega,q)]=\frac{\pi^{2}}{8}(\omega^{2}-q^{2})\left[\coth{\frac{\omega+q}{4T}}+\coth{\frac{\omega-q}{4T}}\right]. (106)

The imaginary part then reads

−Im​ΠR​(H,H)=4​π3​λ2​H​T,-{\rm Im}\Pi^{R}(H,H)=4\pi^{3}\lambda^{2}HT, (107)

giving the width

η=2​π3​λ2​T\eta=2\pi^{3}\lambda^{2}T (108)

Again, this is consistent with the scaling analysis (55). The real part is proportional to (ω2−q2)(\omega^{2}-q^{2}), which corresponds to a wavefunction renormalization, and does not lead to any shift at O⁡(λ2)O(\lambda^{2}). In any case, there is a shift of O⁡(λ)O(\lambda) discussed above, which is dominant.

To summarize, the exchange anisotropy with the axis perpendicular to the applied field gives the following effects on paramagnetic ESR.

shift

+π​λ​H∝H​δ+\pi\lambda H\propto H\delta

width

2​π3​λ2​T∝(δ/J)2​T2\pi^{3}\lambda^{2}T\propto(\delta/J)^{2}T

Comparing to the result for the exchange anisotropy with the axis parallel to the applied field, the width obtained here is half of the result (61) for the parallel case. This can be understood naturally with the MK formula as we will discuss in the next subsection. On the other hand, the shift takes opposite sign and the absolute value is half of that in the parallel case.

VI.2 MK approach

The lineshape is shown to be Lorentzian in the two cases discussed above (exchange anisotropy parallel and perpendicular to the applied field), up to a possible broad background of O⁡(λ2)O(\lambda^{2}). Thus the MK formula is expected to be also valid for these cases. In order to check consistency of our field-theory approach, here we study the same problem with the MK formula.

Let us consider the exchange anisotropy parallel to the applied field considered in Section IV. We may apply the MK formula to the spin chain Hamiltonian and then take the continuum limit, but taking the continuum limit first and then apply the MK formula turns out to be simpler. Absorbing the second term of the effective perturbation (56) into a renormalization of the magnetic field, we need to consider the effect of the perturbation ℋ′∼λ​∫d​x​JLz​JRz{\cal H}^{\prime}\sim\lambda\int dxJ^{z}_{L}J^{z}_{R}.

First we have to obtain the commutator (9) appearing in the MK formula. The total spin raising/lowering operator S±S^{\pm} in the continuum limit is given from eq. (46) as

S±=18​π2​∫d​x​(JR±​e±i​H​x+JL±​e∓i​H​x).S^{\pm}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{8\pi^{2}}}\int dx(J^{\pm}_{R}e^{\pm iHx}+J^{\pm}_{L}e^{\mp iHx}). (109)

Using the standard commutation relation among the currents, the commutator 𝒜{\cal A} is given by

𝒜=i⁡[ℋ′,S+]=i​λ​∫d​x​[JLz​(x)​JR+​(x)​ei​H​x+JRz​(x)​JL+​(x)​e−i​H​x].{\cal A}=i[{\cal H}^{\prime},S^{+}]=i\lambda\int dx[J_{L}^{z}(x)J_{R}^{+}(x)e^{iHx}+J_{R}^{z}(x)J_{L}^{+}(x)e^{-iHx}]. (110)

JLz​JR+J_{L}^{z}J_{R}^{+} and JRz​JL+J_{R}^{z}J_{L}^{+} are primary fields with the conformal weight (1,1)(1,1). Thus, from the MK formula (7) we obtain the linewidth

η=2​λ2χu​H​Im​[−G(1,1)R​(H,H)]\eta=\frac{2\lambda^{2}}{\chi_{u}H}{\rm Im}[-G^{R}_{(1,1)}(H,H)] (111)

The Green’s function is what we have already considered in (106), and thus we obtain the width

η=2​λ2χu​π2​T.\eta=\frac{2\lambda^{2}}{\chi_{u}}\pi^{2}T. (112)

Using eq. (78) again (recall we have set v=1v=1),

η=4​π3​λ2​T.\eta=4\pi^{3}\lambda^{2}T. (113)

This indeed agrees exactly with the result (61) obtained by quite a different approach. We remark that a similar derivation of a similar formula for the ac conductivity of a TL liquid was given earlier by Giamarchi[30].

Next let us consider the exchange anisotropy perpendicular to the applied field. Absorbing the third term in (83) into the renormalization of the magnetic field, the perturbation to be considered is ℋ′=(λ/2)​∫d​x​(JLx​JRx−JLy​JRy−JLz​JRz){\cal H}^{\prime}=(\lambda/2)\int dx(J^{x}_{L}J^{x}_{R}-J^{y}_{L}J^{y}_{R}-J^{z}_{L}J^{z}_{R}). Consequently, the commutator becomes

𝒜=i⁡[ℋ′,S+]=i​λ2​∫d​x​[(JL−​(x)​JRz​(x)+JLz​JR+)​ei​H​x+(JLz​(x)​JR−​(x)+JL+​JRz)​e−i​H​x],{\cal A}=i[{\cal H}^{\prime},S^{+}]=i\frac{\lambda}{2}\int dx[(J_{L}^{-}(x)J_{R}^{z}(x)+J^{z}_{L}J^{+}_{R})e^{iHx}+(J_{L}^{z}(x)J_{R}^{-}(x)+J^{+}_{L}J^{z}_{R})e^{-iHx}], (114)

This leads to

η=λ2χu​H​Im​[−G(1,1)R​(H,H)]=2​π3​λ2​T,\eta=\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\chi_{u}H}{\rm Im}[-G^{R}_{(1,1)}(H,H)]=2\pi^{3}\lambda^{2}T, (115)

where we have used the susceptibility (78) in the second equality. Again we have found an exact agreement with the self-energy approach (108). The ratio 22 of the width between the parallel case (61) and the perpendicular case (108) is simply understood in this approach. It arises from the factor of 1/2 and the presence of twice as many terms in Eq. (114) as compared to Eq. (110). In fact, such an angle dependence also holds at higher temperature and has been discussed in the literature, for example in Refs. 33, 34.

VI.3 Effect of the marginal isotropic operator: logarithmic correction

The Hamiltonian of the Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain with a small anisotropy in the zz direction can be written as

ℋ=ℋ0−[gx​(JRx​JLx+JRy​JLy)+gz​JRz​JLz],{\cal H}={\cal H}_{0}-\left[g^{x}(J^{x}_{R}J^{x}_{L}+J^{y}_{R}J^{y}_{L})+g^{z}J^{z}_{R}J^{z}_{L}\right], (116)

where we ignored the applied field HH, which will be considered later. Here we can rewrite the perturbation as

gx​J→L⋅J→R+(gz−gx)​JLz​JRz,g^{x}\vec{J}_{L}\cdot\vec{J}_{R}+(g^{z}-g^{x})J^{z}_{L}J^{z}_{R}, (117)

where the first term is the isotropic marginal operator. The second term gives the anisotropic interaction λ=−gz+gx\lambda=-g^{z}+g^{x}.

As is now well known, the isotropic marginal perturbation exists in the low-energy effective theory of the Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain, giving several effects such as the logarithmic correction to the magnetic susceptibility[29] at low temperature. While it has a simple form J→L⋅J→R\vec{J}_{L}\cdot\vec{J}_{R} at H=0H=0, it becomes complicated if we include the effect of the applied field HH. It introduces complications such as the momentum non-conservation in the effective theory and the mixing of JxJ^{x} and JyJ^{y}, thereby invalidating the simple self-energy approach discussed in Section V. Thus we actually have no microscopic derivation of the Lorentzian lineshape in the presence of the isotropic marginal operator, at present. On the other hand, the operator by itself, being isotropic, does not directly affect the linewidth. Since the isotropic marginal coupling constant renormalizes to zero, we may expect the Lorentzian lineshape is basically unaffected by its presence. It does, however, indirectly affect the linewidth through the renormalization of the anisotropic perturbation as we discuss in the following.

As discussed in Ref. 42, the coupling constants gxg^{x} and gzg^{z} are renormalized by the Kosterlitz-Thouless type RG flow. The solution of the RG equation (for H=0H=0) in the lowest order gives

gx\displaystyle g^{x} =\displaystyle= ϵ4​π​1sinh⁡(ϵ​ln⁡r)\displaystyle\frac{\epsilon}{4\pi}\frac{1}{\sinh{(\epsilon\ln{r}})} (118)
gz\displaystyle g^{z} =\displaystyle= ϵ4​π​coth⁡(ϵ​ln⁡r),\displaystyle\frac{\epsilon}{4\pi}\coth{(\epsilon\ln{r})}, (119)

where rr is the scale variable (∝J/T\propto J/T) and ϵ\epsilon is a constant, which determines the crossover scale. [This solution is valid only if the infrared (IR) limit is a massless free boson theory, namely if δ<0\delta<0. We proceed by assuming this case; the final result on the ESR linewidth should be valid also for δ>0\delta>0.] In the IR limit r→∞r\rightarrow\infty, gx=0g^{x}=0 and

gz​(∞)=ϵ4​π.g^{z}(\infty)=\frac{\epsilon}{4\pi}. (120)

This corresponds to a renormalized free boson Lagrangian (1−2​π​gz​(∞))​(∂μϕ)2/2(1-2\pi g^{z}(\infty))(\partial_{\mu}\phi)^{2}/2, which leads to the critical exponent ηz=1−2​π​gz​(∞)\eta_{z}=1-2\pi g^{z}(\infty), where ⟨Sz​(r)​Sz​(0)⟩∼r−ηz\langle S^{z}(r)S^{z}(0)\rangle\sim r^{-\eta_{z}}.

On the other hand, the critical exponent in the low-energy limit of the Heisenberg XXZ model has been obtained from the Bethe Ansatz exact solution. For the Heisenberg model with an exchange anisotropy

ℋ=∑jJ⁡(Sjx​Sj+1x+Sjy​Sj+1y)+(J+δ)​Sjz​Sj+1z,{\cal H}=\sum_{j}J(S^{x}_{j}S^{x}_{j+1}+S^{y}_{j}S^{y}_{j+1})+(J+\delta)S^{z}_{j}S^{z}_{j+1}, (121)

it is known that

ηz=12​π​R2=1−1π​cos−1⁡[1+δJ],\eta_{z}=\frac{1}{2\pi R^{2}}=1-\frac{1}{\pi}\cos^{-1}{[1+\frac{\delta}{J}]}, (122)

for a negative δ\delta. Combining these results, we obtain, for small ϵ\epsilon, δ\delta,

ϵ=1π​−8​δJ.\epsilon=\frac{1}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{-8\delta}{J}}. (123)

Since the isotropic part gx​∑αJLα​JRαg^{x}\sum_{\alpha}J^{\alpha}_{L}J^{\alpha}_{R} commutes with S+S^{+}, the important perturbation is the “asymmetric part” gz−gxg^{z}-g^{x}. In the intermediate scale r≪e1/ϵr\ll e^{1/\epsilon}, which would be relevant to ESR for a weak anisotropy,

λ=−gz+gx=18​π​ϵ2​ln⁡r=ln⁡rπ3​δJ.\lambda=-g^{z}+g^{x}=\frac{1}{8\pi}\epsilon^{2}\ln{r}=\frac{\ln{r}}{\pi^{3}}\frac{\delta}{J}. (124)

This corresponds to the coefficient λ\lambda introduced in eq. (54). The larger of the temperature TT or the applied field HH imposes the cutoff of the RG flow, and thus the scale factor rr should be replaced by J/max⁡(T,H)J/{\rm max}(T,H).

In the present discussion, the uniform field HH appears only as a cutoff scale imposed on the RG flow at zero field. Thus, to this order, the renormalization of the coupling constant λ\lambda applies to arbitrary direction of the anisotropy relative to the applied field. Therefore we conclude the low-temperature asymptotic behavior of the linewidth and shift to be

η\displaystyle\eta =\displaystyle= 4π3​(δJ)2​(ln⁡Jmax⁡(T,H))2​T,\displaystyle\frac{4}{\pi^{3}}\left(\frac{\delta}{J}\right)^{2}\left(\ln{\frac{J}{{\rm max}(T,H)}}\right)^{2}T, (125)
Δ​ω\displaystyle\Delta\omega =\displaystyle= −2π2​δJ​ln⁡Jmax⁡(T,H),\displaystyle-\frac{2}{\pi^{2}}\frac{\delta}{J}\ln{\frac{J}{{\rm max}(T,H)}}, (126)

if the anisotropy axis is parallel to the applied field. They are

η\displaystyle\eta =\displaystyle= 2π3​(δJ)2​(ln⁡Jmax⁡(T,H))2​T,\displaystyle\frac{2}{\pi^{3}}\left(\frac{\delta}{J}\right)^{2}\left(\ln{\frac{J}{{\rm max}(T,H)}}\right)^{2}T, (127)
Δ​ω\displaystyle\Delta\omega =\displaystyle= 1π2​δJ​ln⁡Jmax⁡(T,H),\displaystyle\frac{1}{\pi^{2}}\frac{\delta}{J}\ln{\frac{J}{{\rm max}(T,H)}}, (128)

if the anisotropy axis is perpendicular to the applied field. The shift depends on the sign of the anisotropy. When comparing with experiments or existing literature, it should be recalled that we discuss the shift in frequency (for a fixed field HH) while usually a shift in the resonance field for a fixed frequency ω\omega is studied. For example, in the presence of the dipolar interaction, which corresponds to negative δ\delta, when the field is applied parallel to the chain (ie. anisotropy) axis we obtain a positive frequency shift, namely a negative shift in the resonance field. The shift is in the opposite direction when the applied field is perpendicular to the chain axis. These conclusions are qualitatively consistent with the literature. [48, 14]

VI.4 Comparison with experiments

In this paper, we have not calculated the ESR lineshape for a general relative direction between the anisotropy axis and the magnetic field, let alone more complicated anisotropy of general form. However, the results (61), (108) together with the scaling argument (55) imply that the linewidth due to the exchange anisotropy (or dipolar interaction) scales proportionally to the temperature TT in the low temperature regime T≪JT\ll J (but above the Néel or spin-Peierls transition temperature). This, in fact, appears to be observed in many quasi-one dimensional S=1/2S=1/2 antiferromagnets[35, 36, 37, 34, 39, 40] including CPC, KCuF3, CuGeO3 and NaV2O5. In the case of Cu benzoate[10], there is a field-dependent diverging contribution to the linewidth at low temperature due to a staggered field effect, as we will discuss in Section VIII. There seems to be another contribution to the linewidth, which is approximately TT-linear and frequency-independent. We presume the latter contribution is due to the exchange anisotropy.

In Fig. 4 we show the observed[34, 39, 40] ESR linewidth for KCuF3, CuGeO3 and NaV2O5, as a function of the normalized temperature T/JT/J. We note that, these materials exhibit phase transitions (such as Néel and spin-Peierls transitions) at low enough temperatures, where the linewidth appears to diverge. Since we focus on one-dimensional systems in the present work, in Fig. 4 we have omitted such temperature regimes, above which we may regard the system simply as a spin chain. It could be possible that, however, the displayed data are still affected by the interchain interactions, the spin-Peierls instability etc.

An analysis on the linewidth in NaV2O5 similar to ours was published previously by Zvyagin[41]. However, we also remark that the TT-linear behavior of the linewidth due to an exchange anisotropy was reported earlier in Ref. 12. In fact, eq. (3) in Ref. 41 is equivalent to eq. (11) in Ref. 12. Moreover, in Ref. 41 it was argued that a bond-alternation perturbation leads to a linewidth ∝(J1−J2)2/T2\propto(J_{1}-J_{2})^{2}/T^{2}. However, the argument (leading to Eq. (4) in Ref. 41) cannot be correct per se, because the ESR linewidth must remain strictly zero as long as all terms in the Hamiltonian except the Zeeman term commute with the total spin operators, as we reviewed in Sec. II.1. An isotropic bond-alternation has this property. It is possible that an isotropic bond-alternation perturbation (J1−J2)(J_{1}-J_{2}) together with an anisotropic uniform exchange perturbation δ\delta might lead to a width, but it would be suppressed by the factor δ2/J2\delta^{2}/J^{2} as the width should vanish when δ=0\delta=0. In any case, a reliable derivation seems lacking so far. We point out that the ESR spectrum cannot simply be related to the boson propagator in the field theory, in the presence of a bond-alternation. (See remarks below eq. (62).)

In Fig. 4 we took J=400J=400K, 150150K and 560560K respectively[34, 39, 40] for KCuF3, CuGeO3 and NaV2O5, while there are some uncertainties in the estimate. The linewidth is renormalized to be compared with T/JT/J. The low-temperature asymptotic behavior of the linewidth indeed seems consistent, although not perfectly, with the universal TT-linear behavior we have derived. On the other hand, it is difficult to discuss the predicted logarithmic correction in the present data. Regarding Fig. 4 as a fitting, the low-temperature asymptotic behavior reads

ηT∼{4.2×10−4(CuGeO3,H∥c)4.7×10−4(CuGeO3,H∥a)17×10−4(KCuF3,H∥c)22×10−4(KCuF3,H∥a)1.3×10−4(NaV2O5,H∥c)0.65×10−4(NaV2O5,H∥b),\frac{\eta}{T}\sim\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}4.2\times 10^{-4}&(\mbox{CuGeO${}_{3}$},H\parallel c)\\ 4.7\times 10^{-4}&(\mbox{CuGeO${}_{3}$},H\parallel a)\\ 17\times 10^{-4}&(\mbox{KCuF${}_{3}$},H\parallel c)\\ 22\times 10^{-4}&(\mbox{KCuF${}_{3}$},H\parallel a)\\ 1.3\times 10^{-4}&(\mbox{NaV${}_{2}$O${}_{5}$},H\parallel c)\\ 0.65\times 10^{-4}&(\mbox{NaV${}_{2}$O${}_{5}$},H\parallel b)\end{array}\right., (129)

which are given as dimensionless numbers. In these materials, the data for H|aH\parallel a and H|bH\parallel b are quite similar, and thus only one set of them is shown for each material.

Comparing with our results (125) and (127), the anisotropy δ/J\delta/J seems to be about a few percent. It was argued[34, 39, 40] that, in these material it is too (up to 10 times) big compared to what we expect from Moriya’s[27] estimate δ∼(Δ​g/g)2​J\delta\sim(\Delta g/g)^{2}J where Δ​g\Delta g is the anisotropy of the gg-tensor. (Actually the discussion in Refs. 34, 38, 39, 40 was based on the high-temperature limit. See Section IX for relation to our low-temperature theory.) However, we believe that Moriya’s formula is only valid as an order-of-magnitude estimate. There is a room for a factor which is presumably not too much different from 11, but could still allow the exchange anisotropy that is consistent with the observed linewidth.

The linewidth deviates from the field theory result ∝T\propto T at higher temperatures. This is not surprising, since the field theory is only valid in the low temperature T≪JT\ll J. We will give more discussion on the crossover to the high-temperature regime in Section IX. On the other hand, if all the materials can be regarded as standard Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chains with the same type of anisotropy, we would expect the linewidth to be a universal function of T/JT/J. However, in Fig. 4 it is evident that the linewidth behaves differently at high temperature, especially in KCuF3. This suggests that not all of them can be described by the standard Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain (20) with the same type of anisotropy. We remark that the low-temperature asymptotic behavior should be universal for a certain class of Hamiltonians, but the explicit coefficients obtained in eqs. (125) and (127) are specific to the standard Hamiltonian (20).

Certainly, there are many questions still to be understood. An important problem is the dependence on the direction of the applied field. In the case of NaV2O5, the observed linewidth at low temperature is twice as large when H|cH\parallel c compared as when H⟂cH\perp c. This is consistent with our result, if an exchange anisotropy with the single anisotropy axis parallel to cc is assumed. However, in the case of CuGeO3 and KCuF3, the observed linewidth for H|cH\parallel c is smaller than that for H|aH\parallel a and H|bH\parallel b. This kind of angular dependence cannot be explained with an exchange anisotropy with a single anisotropy axis. This suggests that we have to consider more general types of anisotropy, or some other effects.

A complete theoretical description of the experimental data in these materials is left for the future. Nevertheless, we believe that the universal decrease of ESR linewidth at low temperatures in S=1/2S=1/2 antiferromagnetic chains is basically understood with our theory. Ours is presumably the first[12] microscopic derivation of this approximately TT-linear linewidth. In Refs. 34, 38, 39, 40 a completely different interpretation was proposed. However, we will argue against it in Section IX.

VII ESR in an XXZ antiferromagnet

So far in this paper, we have restricted ourselves to the case of small anisotropy. However, in principle ESR can be measured in a system which is far from isotropic. To apply the self-energy formalism to a not small anisotropy, one has to sum up higher orders of the perturbation. In addition, the foundation of our self-energy formalism based on the weakly broken S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry may be questionable in such cases, because the S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry is strongly broken in the spin Hamiltonian.

However, there is one case in which we can study ESR with a strong anisotropy: an easy-plane XXZ antiferromagnet with a field applied perpendicular to the easy plane. This is nothing but the isotropic Heisenberg antiferromagnet with a negative exchange anisotropy parallel to the applied field (121), with δ<0\delta<0. Here we can apply the direct calculation introduced in Sec. IV.

The compactification radius RR for the XXZ model with a given anisotropy δ\delta is known from Bethe Ansatz exact solution and is given in eq. (122). Using this radius, the ESR absorption spectrum given by the Green’s function (38) of the vertex operator with the conformal weight (36),(37). Since δ\delta is not small, the spectrum is no longer a simple Lorentzian, except at low enough temperature T≪H≪JT\ll H\ll J where the spectrum reduces to the Lorentzian (60).

In this Lorentzian case, the width here does not reduce to the previous one (125) which was proportional to δ2\delta^{2}, even in the limit δ→0\delta\rightarrow 0. The reason of this disagreement is that they describe different regimes. The result (125) is valid when the energy scale max⁡(T,H){\rm max}(T,H) is above the crossover energy Ec=e−1/ϵE_{c}=e^{-1/\epsilon}, while the present result is valid if the relevant energy scale TT and HH are both below EcE_{c}. For a small anisotropy, the crossover scale is exponentially small, making eq. (125) realistic for the experimentally accessible regime.

For a small exchange anisotropy and above the crossover energy EcE_{c}, the width is proportional to λ2\lambda^{2} in the leading order of perturbation theory; the width is insensitive to the sign of the anisotropy (easy-plane or easy-axis). However, when the anisotropy is large or T,H≪EcT,H\ll E_{c}, this symmetry no longer holds. In fact, the system in the zero temperature limit is gapless for an easy-plane anisotropy (δ<0\delta<0) while it acquires a gap ∼Ec\sim E_{c} for an easy-axis anisotropy (δ>0\delta>0). In the gapful case δ>0\delta>0 and T,H≪EcT,H\ll E_{c}, ESR probes the creation of the elementary excitation above the groundstate; the absorption spectrum then has a sharp peak centered at the energy of the gap.

VIII Transverse staggered field

As we have discussed in Section III.2, a staggered field is the most relevant perturbation of the isotropic Heisenberg antiferromagnet. Breaking the S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry, the staggered field affects also the ESR spectrum. Here we discuss the effect by the field theory methods described in previous sections, and then explain the mysterious observations in ESR experiments [10, 11] on Cu Benzoate in the 1970’s which were recently confirmed and extended [45].

Let us focus on the case of a transverse staggered field

ℋ′=h​∑j(−1)j​Sjx.{\cal H}^{\prime}=h\sum_{j}(-1)^{j}S^{x}_{j}. (130)

As we have discussed already, the staggered field is mapped to the operator

nx∼k​cos⁡(2​π​R​ϕ~)n^{x}\sim k\cos{(2\pi R\tilde{\phi})} (131)

which has scaling dimension 1/21/2. A standard scaling analysis similar to that in Section IV shows that, ignoring the logarithmic correction, the linewidth should be given as

η=T​g​(EgT,HT),\eta=Tg(\frac{E_{g}}{T},\frac{H}{T}), (132)

where EgE_{g} is the excitation gap[6, 7] due to the staggered field proportional to h2/3​J1/3h^{2/3}J^{1/3}. Again, the scaling argument alone cannot determine the actual form of the scaling function gg.

VIII.1 Self-energy approach

As we have discussed, The staggered transverse field (130) is mapped to the field theory operator nxn^{x}:

ℋ′=h​∑j(−1)j​Sjx∼k​h​∫nx​(r)​𝑑r{\cal H}^{\prime}=h\sum_{j}(-1)^{j}S^{x}_{j}\sim kh\int n^{x}(r)dr (133)

where kk is a constant, and we normalize nxn^{x} by ⟨nx​(r)​nx​(0)⟩=1/r\langle n^{x}(r)n^{x}(0)\rangle=1/r. Namely, k2k^{2} gives the correlation amplitude ⟨S0x​Sjx⟩∼(−1)j​k2/j\langle S^{x}_{0}S^{x}_{j}\rangle\sim(-1)^{j}k^{2}/j. This form is not affected by the application of the magnetic field HH, except for the possible renormalization of the amplitude kk and the exponent, which we will ignore.

The S​U​(2)SU(2) WZW field theory with the perturbation nxn^{x} has rotational symmetry about the xx-axis. While the original spin problem is not invariant under a rotation about the xx-axis due to the applied field, the effective field theory does have this symmetry. As a consequence, correlation functions of the type ⟨Jx​Jy⟩\langle J^{x}J^{y}\rangle vanishes. Thus we can apply the self-energy method by reducing the ESR spectrum to Green’s function of the bosonic field, as discussed in Section V.

The transverse staggered field in the xx direction breaks the rotational symmetry in the x​yxy-plane, leading to polarization dependence. Calculations similar to those in Section VI lead to the same result (98),(99) and (100). The polarization dependence is again consistent with the rigorous relation (18) which can be applied to the present case.

The self-energy Π\Pi is now replaced by the boson self-energy in the presence of the perturbation k​h​cos⁡2​π​ϕkh\cos{\sqrt{2\pi}\phi}. Again, arguments similar to those in Section VI can be applied to obtain the result

ΠR​(ω,q)=2​π​(k​h)2​[G(1/4,1/4)R​(ω,q)−G(1/4,1/4)R​(0,0)],\Pi^{R}(\omega,q)=2\pi(kh)^{2}[G^{R}_{(1/4,1/4)}(\omega,q)-G^{R}_{(1/4,1/4)}(0,0)], (134)

where the second term comes from the tadpole term.

The self-energy is a smooth function of ω\omega near the resonance ω∼H\omega\sim H. Thus, the lineshape is Lorentzian near the center of the resonance, with the width and shift determined by the self-energy at (ω,q)=(H,H)(\omega,q)=(H,H). The imaginary part of the second, tadpole term vanishes according to eq. (38). Using eq. (80), the linewidth is given by

η=π​k2​h2H​Im​[−G(1/4,1/4)R​(H,H)].\eta=\frac{\pi k^{2}h^{2}}{H}{\rm Im}\left[-G^{R}_{(1/4,1/4)}(H,H)\right]. (135)

From eq. (38), the linewidth shows quite a nontrivial dependence on the applied field HH and temperature TT. However, in the weak field regime H≪TH\ll T, the formula can be simplified and linewidth has simple T−2T^{-2} dependence on the temperature.

η=π​k24​(Γ⁡(14)Γ⁡(34))2​h2T2.\eta=\frac{\pi k^{2}}{4}\left(\frac{\Gamma(\frac{1}{4})}{\Gamma(\frac{3}{4})}\right)^{2}\frac{h^{2}}{T^{2}}. (136)

We note that this is consistent with the scaling analysis. (Recall that we have set v=1v=1.)

The correlation amplitude k2k^{2} was recently determined exactly for the S=1/2S=1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet[43, 42, 44] with a logarithmic correction due to the presence of marginal operators:

(−1)r​⟨Sz​(r)​Sz​(0)⟩∼1(2​π)3/2​ln⁡rr.(-1)^{r}\langle S^{z}(r)S^{z}(0)\rangle\sim\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3/2}}\frac{\ln{r}}{r}. (137)

The logarithmic correction is translated into a ln⁡(J/T)\ln{(J/T)} factor in the ESR, where the temperature gives the IR cutoff. Thus we obtain (upon reinstating v=π​J/2v=\pi J/2)

η=116​π2​(Γ⁡(14)Γ⁡(34))2​J​h2T2​ln⁡(JT)∼0.685701​J​h2T2​ln⁡(JT).\eta=\frac{1}{16}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(\frac{\Gamma(\frac{1}{4})}{\Gamma(\frac{3}{4})}\right)^{2}\frac{Jh^{2}}{T^{2}}\ln{(\frac{J}{T})}\sim 0.685701\frac{Jh^{2}}{T^{2}}\ln{(\frac{J}{T})}. (138)

Implication of this result on the experiments will be discussed in Sec. VIII.4.

VIII.2 MK approach

Since the lineshape is Lorentzian, the MK formula should be valid also in this case, provided the correlation function is evaluated appropriately. There are two ways to evaluate the commutator (9) appearing in the MK formula: to take the continuum limit before calculating the commutator, or to first calculate the commutator in terms of the original spin variable and then take the continuum limit. We think the former is generally more reliable, since the field theory only deals with universal low-energy phenomena while the Lorentzian assumption of MK formula would be valid at best in the long-time limit. In the present case, the two methods give the same result as we will show below.

Taking the continuum limit first, we calculate the commutator between the field theory operators (133) and (46). The standard relation between the commutator and OPE leads to

𝒜\displaystyle{\cal A} =\displaystyle= [ℋ′,S−]\displaystyle[{\cal H}^{\prime},S^{-}] (139)
=\displaystyle= [h​k​∫nx​(r)​𝑑r,18​π2​∫JR−​(r)​e−i​H​r+JL−​(r)​ei​H​r]\displaystyle[hk\int n^{x}(r)dr,\frac{1}{8\pi^{2}}\int J^{-}_{R}(r)e^{-iHr}+J^{-}_{L}(r)e^{iHr}]
=\displaystyle= (h​k/2)​∫[e−i​2​π​ϕ​e−i​H​r+ei​2​π​ϕ​ei​H​r]​𝑑r\displaystyle(hk/2)\int[e^{-i\sqrt{2\pi}\phi}e^{-iHr}+e^{i\sqrt{2\pi}\phi}e^{iHr}]dr

On the other hand, in the original spin representation, the commutator is easily evaluated as

𝒜=[ℋ′,S−]=h​∑j(−1)j​Sjz,{\cal A}=[{\cal H}^{\prime},S^{-}]=h\sum_{j}(-1)^{j}S^{z}_{j}, (140)

namely the longitudinal staggered field with the coefficient hh. Taking continuum limit, it agrees with (139).

Thus, from the MK formula, the linewidth is given by

η=k2​h22​χu​H​Im​[−G(1/4,1/4)R​(H,H)].\eta=\frac{k^{2}h^{2}}{2\chi_{u}H}{\rm Im}\left[-G^{R}_{(1/4,1/4)}(H,H)\right]. (141)

Again using eq. (78), this agrees exactly with the result (135) obtained in the self-energy approach.

VIII.3 Shift of the resonance frequency

In the present case, there is no shift to first order in hh. In fact, the first term in the MK formula (10) vanishes in the present case. The lowest order shift is thus second order in hh. This is given by either the MK formula (10) or by Re​ΠR​(H,H)/(2​H){\rm Re}\Pi^{R}(H,H)/(2H) in the self-energy approach. Again, both approaches give the same result for the frequency shift:

Δ​ω=η=π​k2​h2H​Re​[−G(1/4,1/4)R​(0,0)+G(1/4,1/4)R​(H,H)].\Delta\omega=\eta=\frac{\pi k^{2}h^{2}}{H}{\rm Re}\left[-G^{R}_{(1/4,1/4)}(0,0)+G^{R}_{(1/4,1/4)}(H,H)\right]. (142)

This is a straightforward consequence of the self-energy approach. On the other hand, the derivation from the MK approach might need an explanation. While the second term proportional to −G(1/4,1/4)R​(H,H)-G^{R}_{(1/4,1/4)}(H,H) just comes from G𝒜𝒜†RG^{R}_{{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}} in the MK formula (10), the first term (proportional to −G(1/4,1/4)R​(0,0)-G^{R}_{(1/4,1/4)}(0,0)) is less obvious. From eq. (140), the commutator in the first term of the MK formula (10) is given by

[𝒜,S−]=h​∑j(−1)j​S−[{\cal A},S^{-}]=h\sum_{j}(-1)^{j}S^{-} (143)

Its expectation value vanishes if evaluated in the absence of the staggered field ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime}. However, taking the staggered field perturbation into account,

⟨[𝒜,S−]⟩=−h2​χs+O⁡(h3),\langle[{\cal A},S^{-}]\rangle=-h^{2}\chi_{s}+O(h^{3}), (144)

where χs\chi_{s} is the (transverse) staggered susceptibility. By the linear response theory, we have

χs=−k2​Re​G(1/4,1/4)R​(0,0),\chi_{s}=-k^{2}{\rm Re}G^{R}_{(1/4,1/4)}(0,0), (145)

which leads to (142), with the replacement of χu\chi_{u} by its zero-temperature limit (78).

For the standard S=1/2S=1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain, we can apply the exact result on the correlation amplitude as we did for the width. We obtain

Δ​ω=18​π2​ln⁡(JT)​J​h2H​T​(Γ⁡(14)Γ⁡(34))2​[1−Γ⁡(34)Γ⁡(14)​Re​{Γ⁡(14−i​H2​π​T)Γ⁡(34−i​H2​π​T)}]\Delta\omega=\frac{1}{8}\sqrt{\pi\over 2}\ln{(\frac{J}{T})}\frac{Jh^{2}}{HT}\left(\frac{\Gamma(\frac{1}{4})}{\Gamma(\frac{3}{4})}\right)^{2}\left[1-\frac{\Gamma(\frac{3}{4})}{\Gamma(\frac{1}{4})}{\rm Re}\left\{{\Gamma(\frac{1}{4}-i\frac{H}{2\pi T})\over\Gamma(\frac{3}{4}-i\frac{H}{2\pi T})}\right\}\right] (146)

For small field HH compared to temperature TT, we obtain by Taylor expansion of the Gamma function

Δ​ω=.344057​J​h2​HT3​ln⁡(JT).\Delta\omega=.344057\frac{Jh^{2}H}{T^{3}}\ln{(\frac{J}{T})}. (147)

(An incorrect prefactor was given in Ref. 12.) Namely, we obtain the positive shift which rapidly increases with decreasing temperature.

The shift in the presence of the staggered gg-tensor was previously discussed by Nagata[46] using the formula

Δ​ω=−12​χu​H​⟨[[S+,ℋ′],S−]⟩.\Delta\omega=-\frac{1}{2\chi_{u}H}\langle[[S^{+},{\cal H}^{\prime}],S^{-}]\rangle. (148)

derived in Refs. 47, 48. (See also Appendix.) In the present case, it is reduced to the expectation value of the staggered field h​∑j(−1)j​Sjxh\sum_{j}(-1)^{j}S^{x}_{j}. The leading order of the shift in the perturbation hh is thus given by

Δ​ω=h22​χu​H​χs,\Delta\omega=\frac{h^{2}}{2\chi_{u}H}\chi_{s}, (149)

where χs\chi_{s} is the staggered susceptibility [46]. The positive frequency shift (ie. negative field shift) was argued to be consistent with the experiment[49, 46]. On the other hand, the theoretical result in Ref. 46 is not in quantitative agreement, partly due to the evaluation of χs\chi_{s} in the high-temperature classical limit. However, we believe that eq. (149) itself is not quite correct even if χs\chi_{s} were evaluated exactly. In fact, eq. (149) differs from ours (142). Interestingly, eq. (149) is equivalent to including only the tadpole contribution in the self-energy approach. The discrepancy becomes particularly important at low magnetic field. In the limit of H→0H\rightarrow 0 at fixed hh and TT (although this limit is not realistic in experiment) the MK/self-energy approach predict the shift linear in HH but (149) gives a diverging shift ∼1/H\sim 1/H, which is presumably unphysical. While eq. (148) captures some physics of the frequency shift, it fails to include more subtle effects of fluctuation, presumably because of the oversimplified ansatz and of not including the long-timescale dynamics.

VIII.4 Comparison with the experiments

The result (138) of the perturbation theory implies an interesting behavior of the ESR linewidth in materials such as Cu benzoate. As we have discussed in Section III.2.1, there an effective transverse staggered field is induced proportionally to the applied field (h=c​Hh=cH), and the proportionality constant cc depends strongly on the direction of the applied field. Thus, the linewidth increases as ∝T−2\propto T^{-2} as the temperature is lowered. Furthermore, it depends on the applied field (or the resonance frequency) HH and on the direction of the applied field. This very characteristic behavior is not expected for the exchange anisotropy. In fact, these features were actually observed[10] nearly 30 years ago in ESR on Cu benzoate and apparently have not been understood until recently. Our results give a natural understanding of these observations[12].

The only unknown parameters in Cu benzoate were two components of DM vector. We have chosen[12]

(Da′′,Dc′′)=(0.13,0.02)​J(D_{a^{\prime\prime}},D_{c^{\prime\prime}})=(0.13,0.02)J (150)

which seemed most reasonable to fit ESR data[10]. It is also roughly consistent with other experiments[7] such as neutron scattering, although not perfectly. This choice of DM vector fit rather nicely the direction dependence (Fig. 1 of Ref. 12), temperature and field dependence (Fig. 2 of Ref. 12). However, we should note that the determination of the logarithmic correction in a practical fitting is a difficult problem; the leading log correction is only valid in the low temperature limit. Our fittings were done setting the logarithmic factor to unity.

There is some discrepancy between the theory and the experiments. We see, in the experimental data, a field(frequency)-independent contribution which appears to be approximately linear in temperature. This is presumably due to effects other than the staggered field. A probable mechanism is the effect of an exchange anisotropy, which gives a linewidth which is TT-linear and independent of the field. If we subtract the field-independent contribution from the experimental data at the price of introducing additional fitting parameters, the agreement becomes better as shown in Fig. 5.

Recently Asano et al. made a detailed experimental study[45] on ESR in Cu benzoate. They also confirmed our prediction on the linewidth at higher field. In addition, they found that, when the temperature is small compared to JJ but not too low, the shift is consistent with our prediction (147). See Fig. 2 of Ref. 45. Moreover, we can read off the proportionality constant from their Fig. 2 as

Δ​ω∼0.053​(HT)3\Delta\omega\sim 0.053(\frac{H}{T})^{3} (151)

for H|cH\parallel c, where Δ​ω\Delta\omega and HH are measured in Tesla while TT is in Kelvin. On the other hand, using the DM vector (150), e find that h=0.095​Hh=0.095H for H|cH\parallel c. Combining this with (147), we the theoretical prediction

Δ​ω∼0.042​(HT)3,\Delta\omega\sim 0.042(\frac{H}{T})^{3}, (152)

where we have again replaced the logarithm ln⁡J/T\ln{J/T} with unity. Considering the subtlety of the logarithmic correction, the agreement between the theory and the experiment is rather good.

Thus our perturbative results agrees well with the experiments. However, at very low temperatures, the lineshape evolves differently than what we expect from the lowest order perturbation theory. This will be discussed in the next subsection.

VIII.5 Resonance at very low temperature

So far, our analysis was perturbative in the staggered field hh. While the perturbation theory seems reasonable for a small staggered field, it eventually fails at lower temperature where the effect of the staggered field is enhanced. In fact, the perturbative expansion turns out to be an expansion in J​h2/T3Jh^{2}/T^{3}, which is divergent at low enough temperature.

The effective field theory describing the S=1/2S=1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain with a staggered field is given by (21) perturbed with (131). As discussed in Ref. 6, this is nothing but the sine-Gordon field theory, which is one of the best understood strongly interacting field theories. Since the interaction term (131) is relevant, the sine-Gordon field theory is massive, ie. has a finite excitation gap EgE_{g} above the groundstate. The elementary excitations of the sine-Gordon model consist of solitons, antisolitons and breathers which are boundstates of a soliton and an antisoliton.

The perturbation theory is expected to be valid only for T≫EgT\gg E_{g}. Here we consider the opposite limit T≪EgT\ll E_{g}, where the system is essentially in the groundstate. Then we obtain quite a different picture. It is still valid that the ESR spectrum is given by the ⟨ϕ​ϕ⟩\langle\phi\phi\rangle Green’s function at frequency and momentum HH. However, we have to consider the zero-temperature Green’s function in a non-perturbative way.

In the present case (β=2​π\beta=\sqrt{2\pi}), the lowest excitations are 1st breather, soliton and antisoliton, which form an S​U​(2)SU(2) triplet. Thus the excitation gap EgE_{g} is identical to the first breather mass M1M_{1}. The boson field ϕ\phi couples to the 1st breather, and thus its propagator is given by

⟨ϕ​ϕ⟩​(ω,q)∼Zϕω2−q2−M12.\langle\phi\phi\rangle(\omega,q)\sim\frac{Z^{\phi}}{\omega^{2}-q^{2}-{M_{1}}^{2}}. (153)

where ZϕZ^{\phi} is the wavefunction renormalization constant obtained exactly[50] as

Zϕ=(1+ν)π​ν22​sin⁡π​ν2exp(−1π∫0π​νtsin⁡tdt),Z^{\phi}=(1+\nu)\frac{\frac{\pi\nu}{2}}{2\sin{\frac{\pi\nu}{2}}}\exp{\left(-\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi\nu}\frac{t}{\sin{t}}dt\right)}, (154)

where ν=β2/(8​π−β2)\nu=\beta^{2}/(8\pi-\beta^{2}). For the present case, ν=1/3\nu=1/3 and thus Zϕ=0.978689Z^{\phi}=0.978689.

From this, we immediately find that the ESR spectrum at zero temperature is given by a delta-function

−Im​GS+​S−R​(ω)≈(H+H2+M12)22​H2+M12​δ​(ω−H2+M12).-{\rm Im}G^{R}_{S^{+}S^{-}}(\omega)\approx{\left(H+\sqrt{H^{2}+M_{1}^{2}}\right)^{2}\over 2\sqrt{H^{2}+M_{1}^{2}}}\delta(\omega-\sqrt{H^{2}+{M_{1}}^{2}}). (155)

Since the wavefunction renormalization ZϕZ^{\phi} is close to unity, the intensity is identical to that of a free resonance.

Thus we obtain a rather complicated behavior of ESR in the presence of the staggered field. As the temperature is lowered, the linewidth increases in the perturbative regime (T≫EgT\gg E_{g}) as we discussed, but at lower temperature (T≪EgT\ll E_{g}) we see a revival of a sharp resonance. The width of the resonance vanishes at zero temperature. At small but finite temperature 0<T≪Eg0<T\ll E_{g}, the resonance may be broadened due to the thermally activated excitations, but presumably the effect is only of the order of the density of such excitations ∼exp(−Eg/T)\sim\exp{(-E_{g}/T)}.

On the other hand, the ESR frequency at zero (or very low) temperature does receive a shift due to the staggered field. Namely, the resonance frequency ω\omega is given by

ω=H2+M12,\omega=\sqrt{H^{2}+{M_{1}}^{2}}, (156)

compared to the Zeeman frequency HH. For small mass M1≪HM_{1}\ll H, the shift is given as

Δ​ω∼M122​H∼1.57878​(ln⁡Jh)1/3​J2/3​h4/3H,\Delta\omega\sim\frac{{M_{1}}^{2}}{2H}\sim 1.57878\left(\ln{\frac{J}{h}}\right)^{1/3}\frac{J^{2/3}h^{4/3}}{H}, (157)

where we used the result of the breather mass (field-induced gap) Eg=M1∼1.77695​[ln⁡(J/h)]1/6​(J​h2)1/3E_{g}=M_{1}\sim 1.77695[\ln{(J/h)}]^{1/6}(Jh^{2})^{1/3} in Refs. 6, 7. Here we emphasize that our self-energy approach is valid beyond the lowest order of perturbation theory, unlike the MK formula. Thus it allows us a non-perturbative analysis such as the above.

Our prediction agrees quite well with the experimental result in Ref. 11, as discussed in Ref. 12. The non-trivial evolution of the lineshape was indeed observed in the experiment in 1970s. Moreover, using the same parameter (150) we have used for the perturbative analysis, we are able to reproduce the direction dependence of the resonance frequency at very low temperature quite well with eq. (156) as shown in Fig. 3 of Ref. 12. However, the data were only shown at fixed temperature and fixed frequency in Ref. 11. Thus several other predictions of our theory could not be compared. After our proposal[12], Asano et al. studied[45] ESR in Cu benzoate at low temperature and at higher field. They confirmed the crossover to the non-perturbative regime, and that the resonance at very low temperature agreed with the prediction (157) for various fields. Moreover, the crossover between the perturbative and the non-perturbative regime occurs at temperature T∼EgT\sim E_{g}, consistently with our picture. The broadening at the non-perturbative regime was also consistent with the picture e−Eg/Te^{-E_{g}/T}

On the other hand, the precise lineshape at the crossover temperature regime T∼EgT\sim E_{g} requires a non-perturbative calculation of the correlation function of the boson field in the sine-Gordon field theory at finite temperature. Despite remarkably many exact results on the theory based on the integrability, calculation of the finite temperature correlation remains an unsolved problem. The ESR lineshape in Cu benzoate provides a set of rather precise experimental data for the finite temperature correlation function in the sine-Gordon field theory. It is hoped that future theoretical progress will enable us to compare theoretical non-perturbative result with the ESR data in the crossover temperature regime T∼EgT\sim E_{g}.

In Ref. 11, the sharp resonance at very low temperature is considered to be the “antiferromagnetic resonance,” which reflects the Néel ordering due to the interchain interaction. In particular, they identified the appearance of the sharp resonance at very low temperature as the Néel transition. However, a recent μ\muSR experiment on Cu benzoate reveals[51] that a Néel ordering does not occur even down to 2020mK. We believe that the evolution of the ESR lineshape is primarily explained within our one-dimensional theory taking the effective staggered field into account. On the other hand, we also note that the interpretation in Ref. 11 is not totally different from ours; the system has a long-range magnetic order in both theories. The difference is that the order is induced spontaneously due to the interchain interaction in Ref. 11 while it is forced externally by the staggered field in our picture. Spin-wave theory can also be applied to the externally ordered state; the resonance at very low temperature would be then identified with the “upper mode” E+E_{+} (see eq. (3.12) of Ref. 7) which has a qualitatively similar dependence on hh and HH to eq. (156). (We thank H. Shiba for pointing this out.) Quantitatively, however, the sine-Gordon field theory is expected to work better for a small staggered field hh.

IX ESR at higher temperatures

In this paper, we have developed a field-theory approach to ESR in quantum spin chains. The field theory is a low-energy effective theory, and is only valid at low temperatures compared to the exchange coupling. Here we would like to consider ESR in the other extreme, namely the high temperature limit using Kubo-Tomita theory. We will also discuss the crossover between the low-temperature and high-temperature regime.

IX.1 Exchange anisotropy

For the exchange anisotropy (53) in a generic direction, the KT formula (12) has been applied to the linewidth in the literature. The result is

η∝δ2J,\eta\propto\frac{\delta^{2}}{J}, (158)

where we have ignored the direction dependence. It is difficult to discuss the intermediate temperature regime either with the existing theories or with our field theory approach. However, our result can be naturally related to the high-temperature limit, assuming a smooth crossover at temperature T∼JT\sim J, namely if the TT-linear behavior (61),(108) is cut off at T∼JT\sim J as shown in Fig. 6. In fact, this simple scenario seems to agree with the experimental results[35, 36, 37, 34, 39, 40] on CPC, KCuF3, CuGeO3 and NaV2O5, which we think the exchange anisotropy (including the dipolar interaction) is the primary mechanism of the broadening. See Fig. 4 for some of the examples.

We note that, while the low-temperature asymptotic behavior described by the field theory is universal, the crossover to the high-temperature regime is expected to be non-universal. The linewidth as a function of the temperature would depend, for example, on the next-nearest-neighbor interaction introduced additionally to the standard Hamiltonian (20).

IX.2 Staggered field

No literature on the effect of a staggered field in ESR linewidth is known to us. The application of the KT formula (12) to the staggered field perturbation (130) is nevertheless straightforward, giving the linewidth

η∝h2J,\eta\propto\frac{h^{2}}{J}, (159)

at the high temperature limit. This is again consistent with the low-temperature field theory result eq. (138), assuming a smooth crossover at T∼JT\sim J, as shown in Fig. 7.

IX.3 Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction

While the effects of a DM interaction (51) has been discussed in the literature[33, 34, 38], we believe there is a rather serious problem with these previous treatments. A direct application of the KT formula (12), as was made previously, yields the width

η∝D2J,\eta\propto\frac{D^{2}}{J}, (160)

where we have again ignored the angle dependence.

On the other hand, a staggered DM interaction can be reduced to an exchange interaction δ∼D2/J\delta\sim D^{2}/J and a transverse staggered field h∼D​H/Jh\sim DH/J via an exact transformation discussed in Sec. III.2.1. If we apply the KT formula after the transformation, we obtain

η∝D4J3+D2​H2J3,\eta\propto\frac{D^{4}}{J^{3}}+\frac{D^{2}H^{2}}{J^{3}}, (161)

where we ignored constants of O⁡(1)O(1). This actually differs substantially from the result of the direct application (160). In a typical situation, D/J∼0.1D/J\sim 0.1 and H≪D<JH\ll D<J so that η∼0.01​J\eta\sim 0.01J from eq. (160) while η∼10−4​J\eta\sim 10^{-4}J from eq. (161), which means a factor of 100100 difference. (Actually we have to know the numerical coefficient, which has been ignored so far, in order to discuss the absolute value of the width.) In addition, it is argued[28] that there exists an exchange anisotropy (before the transformation) which accompanies the DM interaction, and cancels the anisotropy coming from the DM interaction. The discrepancy would be even greater when this happens.

Obviously, both results cannot be true at the same time (while they could be both wrong.) What we believe is that the latter approach eliminating the DM interaction first is appropriate, and the direct application of the KT formula to the DM interaction is incorrect. A possible reason why the direct application (160) fails is as follows. In the latter approach based on the transformation (161), the physical total spin operator Sx,yS^{x,y} is actually given by a sum of the total spin operator and the staggered spin operator of the model after the transformation. Thus, the physical absorption spectrum of ESR is also given by the sum of contributions from the uniform and staggered part:

χphys′′​(q=0,ω)∼χ′′​(q=0,ω)+(DJ)2​χ′′​(q=π,ω),\chi^{\prime\prime}_{\rm phys}(q=0,\omega)\sim\chi^{\prime\prime}(q=0,\omega)+\left(\frac{D}{J}\right)^{2}\chi^{\prime\prime}(q=\pi,\omega), (162)

where χ′′\chi^{\prime\prime} is the imaginary part of the dynamical susceptibility for the transformed model. The staggered part χ′′​(q=π,ω)\chi^{\prime\prime}(q=\pi,\omega) is already broad even in the absence of the anisotropic perturbation, and is further suppressed by the factor (D/J)2(D/J)^{2}. Thus it would be practically indistinguishable from the background, especially in the high temperature regime. The main absorption due to the χ′′​(q=0,ω)\chi^{\prime\prime}(q=0,\omega) term is presumably Lorentzian with the width given by (161). According to this picture, the lineshape is not a single Lorentzian, although apparently it is. The direct application of the KT formula misses such a structure, and treats all the effects as if the lineshape is a single Lorentzian. This presumably leads to the incorrect result (160).

An indirect evidence of our claim is that the elimination seems to work well in the field theory of ESR at low temperature. Assuming a smooth crossover at T∼JT\sim J, the latter result (161) seems more plausible. In addition, a recent experiment[9] on a very good one-dimensional S=1/2S=1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet Pyrimidine Cu dinitrate strongly suggests that there is a staggered DM interaction along the chain, resulting in the field-induced gap similar to that observed in Cu benzoate. An analysis of various experimental data suggests[9] that the staggered DM interaction D∼0.14​JD\sim 0.14J, where the exchange coupling in this compound is J∼36​KJ\sim 36{\rm K}. According to the direct approach (160), the linewidth at high temperature should be of the order of D2/J∼5000​OeD^{2}/J\sim 5000{\rm Oe}. This might be too large to understand the observed small linewidth ∼20​Oe\sim 20{\rm Oe} at room temperature[9], which is quite high compared to the exchange interaction JJ. On the other hand, if we use eq. (161) and H≪DH\ll D, the estimate of the linewidth becomes to be of order of D4/J3∼100​OeD^{4}/J^{3}\sim 100{\rm Oe}, which is not too far from the experimental result. We note that we do not know the numerical coefficients and thus a conclusive quantitative discussion is difficult. In addition, the exchange anisotropy (before the elimination of the DM interaction), which is ignored in the above estimate, is not known precisely. Nevertheless, considering the significant difference, the observed linewidth in pyrimidine Cu dinitrate could serve as an experimental support for our claim that the direct treatment of the DM interaction is inappropriate.

On the other hand, we do not understand at present how to deal with a uniform DM interaction along the chain. While it can be eliminated by a similar transformation as well, the result contains the magnetic field rotating in its direction along the chain. This is a rather unfamiliar problem which we do not know how to handle at present.

IX.4 High-temperature expansion of the linewidth

In a series of papers, Yamada and collaborators studied the temperature dependence of ESR linewidth in one dimensional magnetic systems experimentally and theoretically. In the theoretical study, they discussed the temperature dependence by a high-temperature expansion of the KT formula. More precisely, they attempted a high-temperature expansion of ⟨𝒜𝒜†⟩\langle{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}\rangle in the numerator of the KT formula, Eq. (12).

They concluded that for an exchange anisotropy the linewidth increases as the temperature is lowered, while the tendency is the opposite for a (uniform or staggered) DM interaction. Based on this observation, they argued that the DM interaction should be dominant in several one-dimensional antiferromagnets which showed a decreasing linewidth at lower temperature. In some cases the DM interaction is forbidden according to the previously identified crystal symmetry; they went on to the conclusion that the actual symmetry is lower than what had been believed, allowing the DM interaction.

However, their argument is to be criticized on several grounds. First, the high-temperature expansion can not be trusted except for very high temperature. At T≪JT\ll J our field theory approach should be more reliable, and it gives a rather opposite result to their claim. Second, they expand only the numerator ⟨𝒜𝒜†⟩\langle{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}\rangle in the KT formula to the first order in 1/T1/T, ignoring other possible contributions of order 1/T1/T. It is not clear to us whether their scheme makes sense as a 1/T1/T expansion of the linewidth. Third, perhaps most importantly, even in their framework of the calculation, the conclusion should be reversed because they apparently made a crucial sign mistake as we will show below. Finally, they apply the KT formula directly to the DM interaction; this is problematic as we have pointed out. In any case, the sign problem persists whether the direct approach or the elimination approach is taken in dealing with the DM term.

In the following, let us show that the sign should be reversed within the framework of Refs. 34, 38, 39, 40. We consider S=1/2S=1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chains with a small perturbation. First let us discuss the case of an anisotropy parallel to the applied field. The calculation for general anisotropy angle should be similar. This gives the commutator

𝒜=[ℋ′,S+]=δ​∑j(Sj+​Sj+1z+Sjz​Sj+1+).{\cal A}=[{\cal H}^{\prime},S^{+}]=\delta\sum_{j}(S^{+}_{j}S^{z}_{j+1}+S^{z}_{j}S^{+}_{j+1}). (163)

The “numerator” of the KT formula is then given by

⟨𝒜𝒜†⟩=δ2​∑j,k⟨(Sj+​Sj+1z+Sjz​Sj+1+)​(Sk−​Sk+1z+Skz​Sk+1−)⟩.\langle{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}\rangle=\delta^{2}\sum_{j,k}\langle(S^{+}_{j}S^{z}_{j+1}+S^{z}_{j}S^{+}_{j+1})(S^{-}_{k}S^{z}_{k+1}+S^{z}_{k}S^{-}_{k+1})\rangle. (164)

Considering the high-temperature limit we can ignore all but nearest-neighbor correlations. Thus we only consider the j=kj=k terms in the double sum;

⟨[ℋ′,S+]​[S−,ℋ′]⟩∼δ2​N​[14+⟨Sz⟩2+⟨Sjx​Sj+1x⟩],\langle[{\cal H}^{\prime},S^{+}][S^{-},{\cal H}^{\prime}]\rangle\sim\delta^{2}N[\frac{1}{4}+\frac{\langle S^{z}\rangle}{2}+\langle S^{x}_{j}S^{x}_{j+1}\rangle], (165)

where we have used identities for S=1/2S=1/2, such as Sj+​Sj−=Sjz+1/2S^{+}_{j}S^{-}_{j}=S^{z}_{j}+1/2 and NN is the number of sites. In the limit of infinite temperature, the width is given by the first term which is δ2/J\delta^{2}/J as was already discussed.

As the temperature is lowered from infinity, the leading correction is given by the second and third terms. The second term proportional to the magnetization ⟨Sz⟩\langle S^{z}\rangle is negligible compared to the third term in our case H≪JH\ll J. The third term represents the nearest-neighbor correlation effect, and should be proportional to −J/T-J/T at high temperature TT. Note that we are dealing with an antiferromagnet, so that the nearest-neighbor correlation should be negative. Ignoring other possible sources of temperature dependence following Refs. 34, 38, 39, 40, the linewidth in the present case is given by

η=δ2J​[a−b​JT+O⁡(J2T2)],\eta=\frac{{\delta}^{2}}{J}[a-b\frac{J}{T}+O(\frac{J^{2}}{T^{2}})], (166)

with positive coefficients a,ba,b for an antiferromagnet. Namely, the linewidth decreases at lower temperature contrary to the claims made in Refs. 34, 38, 39, 40; this is rather natural from the field theory results at low temperatures as discussed in Section IX.1. It appears that, they took the nearest-neighbor correlation as positive, which is valid for a ferromagnet[52] but not for an antiferromagnet.

Now let us consider the transverse staggered field perturbation in the same framework. In this case, 𝒜=[ℋ′,S+]=−h∑j(−1)jSjz{\cal A}=[{\cal H}^{\prime},S^{+}]=-h\sum_{j}(-1)^{j}S^{z}_{j}, which gives the “numerator”

⟨𝒜𝒜†⟩=h2​∑j,k(−1)j+k​⟨Sjz​Skz⟩.\langle{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}\rangle=h^{2}\sum_{j,k}(-1)^{j+k}\langle S^{z}_{j}S^{z}_{k}\rangle. (167)

In the high-temperature limit, we may ignore all the correlation functions other than the nearest neighbor one. This leads to the formula

⟨𝒜𝒜†⟩=h2​N​[14−2​⟨Sjz​Sj+1z⟩]\langle{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}\rangle=h^{2}N[\frac{1}{4}-2\langle S^{z}_{j}S^{z}_{j+1}\rangle] (168)

Considering that the nearest-neighbor correlation is negative for an antiferromagnet, the linewidth is supposed to be given as

η=h2J​[a′+b′​JT+O⁡(J2T2)],\eta=\frac{h^{2}}{J}[a^{\prime}+b^{\prime}\frac{J}{T}+O(\frac{J^{2}}{T^{2}})], (169)

where a′a^{\prime} and b′b^{\prime} are positive constants. Namely, the linewidth increases at lower temperature; again in a qualitative agreement with the field theory.

For a staggered DM interaction, as we have discussed before, presumably we should first eliminate the DM interaction to reduce the problem to the exchange anisotropy and the transverse staggered field. In a typical situation H≪D≪JH\ll D\ll J, the staggered field h∼D​H/Jh\sim DH/J and the anisotropy δ∼D2/J\delta\sim D^{2}/J induced by the transformation satisfy h≪δ≪Jh\ll\delta\ll J. In this case, the linewidth would initially decrease by lowering the temperature, then start increasing below the crossover temperature where the staggered field becomes dominant. This was actually observed in Cu benzoate, as discussed already in Section VIII.4.

Finally, we consider a direct application of the KT formula to the DM interaction. Although we believe this is not an adequate approach, the claims in Refs. 34, 38, 39, 40 still suffers from the same sign problem even if we accept the direct approach. Now we have

𝒜=[ℋ′,S+]=∑jDj​i​(Sjz​Sj+1+−Sj+​Sj+1z),{\cal A}=[{\cal H}^{\prime},S^{+}]=\sum_{j}D_{j}i(S^{z}_{j}S^{+}_{j+1}-S^{+}_{j}S^{z}_{j+1}), (170)

giving

⟨𝒜𝒜†⟩∼D2​N​[1−⟨Sjx​Sj+1x⟩],\langle{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}\rangle\sim D^{2}N[1-\langle S^{x}_{j}S^{x}_{j+1}\rangle], (171)

ignoring other than next-nearest-neighbor correlation in the high-temperature limit. Because the nearest neighbor correlation function is negative in an antiferromagnet, we obtain

η=D2J​[a′′+b′′​JT+O⁡(J2T2)],\eta=\frac{D^{2}}{J}[a^{\prime\prime}+b^{\prime\prime}\frac{J}{T}+O(\frac{J^{2}}{T^{2}})], (172)

where a′′a^{\prime\prime} and b′′b^{\prime\prime} are positive constants, implying the increasing linewidth at lower temperatures. The error in Refs. 34, 38, 39, 40 is again apparently due to the identification of the nearest-neighbor correlation as positive.

X Conclusions

In this paper, we have developed a new approach based on field theory to ESR in quantum spin chains. It is expected to be exact in the low-energy (low-temperature) limit, precisely where the traditional calculational methods on ESR become invalid. The weakly broken S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry under an applied field, in the absence of an anisotropic perturbation, is represented by the S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetric field theory and an anisotropic mapping between the physical spin operators and the corresponding field theory operators.

The formulation of the ESR in terms of Feynman-Dyson self-energy gives, at least in some simple cases, a microscopic derivation of the Lorentzian lineshape up to a possible smooth weak background. The spin diffusion picture[4], which predicts a non-Lorentzian lineshape in one dimension, does not apply to the S=1/2S=1/2 antiferromagnetic chain at low temperature. The spin diffusion hypothesis does not hold in the present case, as the spin correlation function is given explicitly using eq. (38).

The width and shift are calculated perturbatively for a transverse staggered field perturbation and an exchange anisotropy parallel or perpendicular to the applied uniform field. They seem to explain many existing experimental data. Furthermore, the self-energy formulation can be used beyond the perturbation theory. In fact, in the presence of a staggered field, the perturbation theory breaks down at a low enough temperature. The ESR spectrum in the zero temperature limit is discussed with a non-perturbative treatment of the sine-Gordon field theory. This again seem to explain the experimentally observed ESR lineshape in Cu benzoate at very low temperature.

While our field theory approach works only at low temperatures, we have also discussed a few aspects of ESR at higher temperatures. In particular, we have pointed out that a naive application of the standard Kubo-Tomita theory fails even in the high temperature limit, in the presence of a Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction.

We hope that the reader is convinced that ESR in a strongly interacting quantum system is quite an interesting problem from the theoretical point of view. It is also a useful experimental probe because a very precise spectrum can be obtained.

Obviously, there remain many problems to be investigated in the future. Even in the simple quantum antiferromagnetic chain, the formulation of ESR in terms of self-energy of the boson field ϕ\phi does not hold for generic types of anisotropic perturbations, because of the mixing of several operators. Extension of the self-energy formulation to the generic cases is an important open problem; presumably we have to consider perturbative expansion of correlation functions of the vertex operators (exponentials of the boson field) in a systematic way. Moreover, degrees of freedom other than spins (e.g. charge fluctuation, lattice vibration etc.) will be relevant in some real materials. While the ESR in a three-dimensional magnet appears to be understood with the existing theory[2, 3], we think that the problem should be reinvestigated with the modern understanding of many-body physics and critical phenomena. Naturally, the two-dimensional problem, which is expected to be more sensitive to the fluctuation effects, would also deserve consideration. We hope the present work will stimulate further theoretical and experimental studies on this fascinating subject.

Note Added. After submitting the present paper, a paper by Choukroun, Richard and Stepanov was published[53]. They made a similar proposal to ours (Sec. IX.3 in the present paper) on the treatment of the Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction at high temperature limit.

Appendix A Alternative derivation of the Mori-Kawasaki formula

In this appendix, we describe a simple alternative derivation of the MK formula (7),(10) suggested to us by David M. Edwards. It depends only on the assumption that the lineshape takes a single Lorentzian form, and appears much simpler than that in the original paper[2]. On the other hand, it does not answer the question why (and when) the lineshape takes the Lorentzian form.

We consider ESR in a general spin system given by the Hamiltonian (6). Here and in the following, a spin operator without a site index is regarded as the total spin operator Sα=∑jSjαS^{\alpha}=\sum_{j}S^{\alpha}_{j}. The equations of motion for S±S^{\pm} are given by

d​S+d​t\displaystyle\frac{dS^{+}}{dt} =\displaystyle= −i​H​S++i​𝒜\displaystyle-iHS^{+}+i{\cal A} (173)
d​S−d​t\displaystyle\frac{dS^{-}}{dt} =\displaystyle= +i​H​S−−i​𝒜†,\displaystyle+iHS^{-}-i{\cal A}^{\dagger}, (174)

where 𝒜=[ℋ′,S+]{\cal A}=[{\cal H}^{\prime},S^{+}].

The ESR spectrum can be obtained from the Green’s function of S±S^{\pm}. Let us relate this to the Green’s function of 𝒜{\cal A} and 𝒜†{\cal A}^{\dagger}, using the equations of motion. Using a partial integration and the equations of motion,

𝒢S+​S−R​(ω)\displaystyle{\cal G}^{R}_{S^{+}S^{-}}(\omega) =\displaystyle= −i∫0∞ei​ω​t⟨[S+(t),S−(0)]⟩dt\displaystyle-i\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{i\omega t}\langle[S^{+}(t),S^{-}(0)]\rangle dt (175)
=\displaystyle= 1ω​⟨[S+​(0),S−​(0)]⟩+1ω​∫0∞ei​ω​t​⟨[d​S+d​t​(t),S−​(0)]⟩​𝑑t\displaystyle\frac{1}{\omega}\langle[S^{+}(0),S^{-}(0)]\rangle+\frac{1}{\omega}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{i\omega t}\langle[\frac{dS^{+}}{dt}(t),S^{-}(0)]\rangle dt
=\displaystyle= 2​⟨Sz⟩ω+Hω​𝒢S+​S−R​(ω)−1ω​𝒢𝒜​S−R​(ω).\displaystyle\frac{2\langle S^{z}\rangle}{\omega}+\frac{H}{\omega}{\cal G}^{R}_{S^{+}S^{-}}(\omega)-\frac{1}{\omega}{\cal G}^{R}_{{\cal A}S^{-}}(\omega).

Thus

𝒢S+​S−R​(ω)=2​⟨Sz⟩−𝒢𝒜​S−Rω−H.{\cal G}^{R}_{S^{+}S^{-}}(\omega)=\frac{2\langle S^{z}\rangle-{\cal G}^{R}_{{\cal A}S^{-}}}{\omega-H}. (176)

(Precisely speaking we should introduce the convergence factor so that ω−H\omega-H is replaced by ω−H+i​ϵ\omega-H+i\epsilon with a positive infinitesimal ϵ\epsilon. Although we omit this for brevity, it can be recovered when necessary.) Performing similar steps,

𝒢𝒜​S−R​(ω)\displaystyle{\cal G}^{R}_{{\cal A}S^{-}}(\omega) =\displaystyle= −i∫0∞ei​ω​t⟨[𝒜(t),S−(0)]⟩dt\displaystyle-i\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{i\omega t}\langle[{\cal A}(t),S^{-}(0)]\rangle dt (177)
=\displaystyle= 1ω​⟨[𝒜⁡(0),S−​(0)]⟩−1ω​∫0∞ei​ω​t​⟨[𝒜⁡(t),d​S−d​t​(0)]⟩​𝑑t\displaystyle\frac{1}{\omega}\langle[{\cal A}(0),S^{-}(0)]\rangle-\frac{1}{\omega}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{i\omega t}\langle[{\cal A}(t),\frac{dS^{-}}{dt}(0)]\rangle dt
=\displaystyle= +⟨[𝒜⁡(0),S−​(0)]⟩ω+Hω​𝒢𝒜​S−R​(ω)−1ω​𝒢𝒜𝒜†R​(ω),\displaystyle+\frac{\langle[{\cal A}(0),S^{-}(0)]\rangle}{\omega}+\frac{H}{\omega}{\cal G}^{R}_{{\cal A}S^{-}}(\omega)-\frac{1}{\omega}{\cal G}^{R}_{{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}}(\omega),

where we used the relation

dd​t​⟨[𝒜⁡(t),S−​(0)]⟩=−⟨[𝒜⁡(t),d​S−d​t​(0)]⟩\frac{d}{dt}\langle[{\cal A}(t),S^{-}(0)]\rangle=-\langle[{\cal A}(t),\frac{dS^{-}}{dt}(0)]\rangle (178)

which holds because the Green’s function depends only on the difference of two time arguments. Thus

𝒢𝒜​S−R​(ω)=⟨[𝒜⁡(0),S−​(0)]⟩−𝒢𝒜𝒜†R​(ω)ω−H.{\cal G}^{R}_{{\cal A}S^{-}}(\omega)=\frac{\langle[{\cal A}(0),S^{-}(0)]\rangle-{\cal G}^{R}_{{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}}(\omega)}{\omega-H}. (179)

Combining eqs. (176) and (179), we obtain

𝒢S+​S−R​(ω)=2​⟨Sz⟩ω−H+−⟨[𝒜⁡(0),S−​(0)]⟩+𝒢𝒜𝒜†R​(ω)(ω−H)2.{\cal G}^{R}_{S^{+}S^{-}}(\omega)=\frac{2\langle S^{z}\rangle}{\omega-H}+\frac{-\langle[{\cal A}(0),S^{-}(0)]\rangle+{\cal G}^{R}_{{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}}(\omega)}{(\omega-H)^{2}}. (180)

This should be an exact relation between the full Green’s functions (in which the effect of the perturbation ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime} is fully taken into account.) When ℋ′=0{\cal H}^{\prime}=0, we recover the simple result 𝒢S+​S−R​(ω)=2​⟨Sz⟩/(ω−H){\cal G}^{R}_{S^{+}S^{-}}(\omega)=2\langle S^{z}\rangle/(\omega-H).

Now let us assume the perturbation ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime} is small, and the ESR lineshape is Lorentzian. Namely, we assume that 𝒢S+​S−R​(ω){\cal G}^{R}_{S^{+}S^{-}}(\omega) is given by eq. (11) where Σ\Sigma is a smooth function of ω\omega. Near the resonance ω∼H\omega\sim H, Σ\Sigma may be regarded as a constant. Re​Σ{\rm Re}\Sigma and −Im​Σ-{\rm Im}\Sigma gives the shift and width of the resonance, respectively. We assume that Σ\Sigma can be expanded perturbatively in ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime}.

Comparing eqs. (11) and (180), we obtain, in the lowest order of perturbation theory,

Σ∼−⟨[𝒜⁡(0),S−​(0)]⟩+𝒢𝒜𝒜†R​(ω=H)2​⟨Sz⟩.\Sigma\sim\frac{-\langle[{\cal A}(0),S^{-}(0)]\rangle+{\cal G}^{R}_{{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}}(\omega=H)}{2\langle S^{z}\rangle}. (181)

Here we note that ⟨[𝒜⁡(0),S−​(0)]⟩\langle[{\cal A}(0),S^{-}(0)]\rangle is purely real since [𝒜,S−][{\cal A},S^{-}] is Hermitean. This gives

η\displaystyle\eta =\displaystyle= −12​⟨Sz⟩​Im​𝒢𝒜𝒜†R​(ω=H),\displaystyle\frac{-1}{2\langle S^{z}\rangle}{\rm Im}{\cal G}^{R}_{{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}}(\omega=H), (182)
Δ​ω\displaystyle\Delta\omega =\displaystyle= 12​⟨Sz⟩​[−⟨[𝒜,S−]⟩+Re​𝒢𝒜𝒜†R​(ω=H)].\displaystyle\frac{1}{2\langle S^{z}\rangle}\left[-\langle[{\cal A},S^{-}]\rangle+{\rm Re}{\cal G}^{R}_{{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}}(\omega=H)\right]. (183)

For a small field HH, the denominator 2​⟨Sz⟩2\langle S^{z}\rangle can be written as 2​χu​H2\chi_{u}H where χu\chi_{u} is the uniform susceptibility. We also note that the first term in the shift −⟨[𝒜,S−]⟩/(2⟨Sz⟩)-\langle[{\cal A},S^{-}]\rangle/(2\langle S^{z}\rangle) was derived previously by Kanamori and Tachiki[47], and by Nagata and Tazuke[48]. However, their theory did not incorporate the dynamical effects represented by 𝒢𝒜𝒜†R{\cal G}^{R}_{{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}}.

So far, we have defined the expectation value and the Green’s functions with respect to the full Hamiltonian ℋ=ℋ0+ℋZ+ℋ′{\cal H}={\cal H}_{0}+{\cal H}_{Z}+{\cal H}^{\prime}. However, the present result is only valid in the leading order. Since the Green’s function of 𝒜{\cal A} above already contains the factor λ2\lambda^{2} (λ\lambda is the small parameter that characterizes the perturbation ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime}), we may replace 𝒢𝒜𝒜†R{\cal G}^{R}_{{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}} with the unperturbed Green’s function G𝒜𝒜†RG^{R}_{{\cal A}{\cal A}^{\dagger}}. This gives the formulae in eqs. (7) and (10). We note that, in general, ⟨[𝒜,S−]⟩\langle[{\cal A},S^{-}]\rangle must still be evaluated in the presence of ℋ′{\cal H}^{\prime} because [𝒜,S−][{\cal A},S^{-}] is only first order in λ\lambda.
